Each edition numbers a court's municipalities in its own alphabetical order, so municipality 23 of Trutnov in Czech is 1 in German, and the municipalities of one Czech page fall on two or three German scans. A municipality is paired when its two printed names share a form — ``Pilníkov, Pilnikau`` and ``Pilnikau, Pilnikov`` — inside the same court, one to one, and a name that would pair with two municipalities is refused rather than given to either. **The unit is the municipality, not the settlement.** Parts are numbered within a municipality in the edition's own order too, and the two editions do not always split a municipality into the same parts, so a settlement-level pairing would be a second name join on worse names. The second is the one that matters: two readers who both find one glyph hard err together on it while erring independently given the glyph, and pooling over glyphs reads that as dependence. Only the Czech volume has one. German Bohemia, Moravia and Silesia are scans with at most a plain or position-less text layer, and a crown-land volume not yet acquired may have nothing at all. This module reads the same geometry off the pixels, so that a volume can be cut into crops without any OCR: the frame and the table's column rules , from long vertical runs of ink; the header row between the table's top rule and the double rule under it, and the column schema it implies: how many columns, and which of them a spanning label groups together (a horizontal rule inside the header); the table foot , where the interior column rules stop; the apparatus divider — the short central rule below the table — and the two columns it opens; the footer band below the divider's foot, down to the last printed line; section headings inside each apparatus column. A heading is a line set centred in its column with white on both sides and a blank line above, whereas an entry opens at the column's left edge and a wrapped entry line at the hanging indent. Found by projection: no character is read, so a heading the OCR loses (scans 0090 0141 0190 0241 0304 0384 0456 of the Czech volume) is still a heading here; blank rows , where a strip cut can fall without passing through ink. Opt-in only. Nothing in the existing pipeline calls this module, and no default anywhere changes because it exists. It is measured against the ALTO geometry on the Czech volume ( utils/lexikon_1910/_archive/measure_image_geometry.py ) and its crops are checked for lost print by ink accounting ( utils/lexikon_1910/_archive/measure_ink_accounting.py ). Making it the default is a separate decision, gated on a re-read (see the hand-over). All pixel thresholds are written at the scale of the Czech render — the ALTO frame, 2,928 px wide — and multiplied by PageGeometry.scale , which is the ratio of this page's frame (or, before the frame is found, its width) to that reference. For a birthplace-level covariate this is the richest thing in the volume: it measures institutional presence , not demography. It arrives in two forms in the same sentence, and the split decides what can be read from a text layer at all: Abbreviations — o. hjtm. , b. úř. , gymn. , měšť. šk. , kl. , elektrárna , and the single-letter cooperative codes. Plain text. This module decodes them against reference/places/institution_abbreviations.csv . Pictograms — obecná škola, doctor, pharmacy, fire brigade, post. The OCR renders these as glyph noise ( Щ1 , gg§! , ф ) and no amount of parsing recovers a symbol the engine never identified. The pictograms are emitted anyway, as unresolved slots. The text layer still knows a marker was printed and where, so each one becomes a row with its page and position and an empty code . That makes the eventual vision pass a join — ship the crops, get codes back, fill the column — rather than a re-parse of everything. Designing it in now costs one column; retrofitting it later would mean re-running the whole extraction. Measured 2026-08-06, and it breaks that plan: the slots are not all the markers. Over the 20-page pilot the text layer emits 291 unresolved slots where the image reads find 893 printed symbols (glm-ocr) and 545 (qwen3.5) — a threefold undercount, with only 16 of 221 municipality entries agreeing exactly and 185 holding more symbols than the ALTO saw. The cause is visible in _GLYPH_RE , which can only recognise a marker that OCR'd into something that is not a letter. A pictogram the engine rendered as Щ , ф or $ becomes a slot; the same pictogram rendered as g , f , p or S — which is the commoner outcome — is indistinguishable from type and is never emitted at all. Page 270 prints four symbols in 1, 1) [school] II, [doctor], [fire-brigade], [cooperative]: R ; the ALTO gives g II, $, f, R. and yields one slot. So "the text layer knows where every marker is, the image read knows what it is" is false, and which third it knows is decided by how the OCR happened to fail. join_symbols can still fill a slot, but its count guard cannot be a gate: the two channels are not counting the same thing, so a disagreement is the normal case and not evidence about the reader. For the offices sections the image read has to be the primary record and this module's slots a lower bound — which moves the burden of proof onto two independent readers agreeing ( compare_passes ) rather than onto agreement with the ALTO. Two cautions that come from the source rather than from the code: The two editions disagree on letters. A building cooperative is St in the Czech volume and B in the German. Never join the editions on the letter. The language suffix is the point and it does not survive. Hč versus Hn marks a cooperative as Czech or German — an ethnic-institutional variable with no equivalent in the census — and the OCR keeps it on 2 occurrences in 188. It is recorded as language_suffix where present and left empty otherwise, never guessed. """Decode the ``Úřady, ústavy`` footnote into an institution inventory. The third footnote block lists, per municipality, what the place actually had — a district court, a tax office, a notary, schools, a deanery, a power station, a brewery, cooperatives. For a birthplace-level covariate this is the richest thing in the volume: it measures *institutional presence*, not demography. It arrives in two forms in the same sentence, and the split decides what can be read from a text layer at all: * **Abbreviations** — ``o. hjtm.``, ``b. úř.``, ``gymn.``, ``měšť. šk.``, ``kl.``, ``elektrárna``, and the single-letter cooperative codes. Plain text. This module decodes them against ``reference/places/institution_abbreviations.csv``. * **Pictograms** — obecná škola, doctor, pharmacy, fire brigade, post. The OCR renders these as glyph noise (``Щ1``, ``gg§!``, ``ф``) and no amount of parsing recovers a symbol the engine never identified. **The pictograms are emitted anyway, as unresolved slots.** The text layer still knows a marker was printed and where, so each one becomes a row with its page and position and an empty ``code``. That makes the eventual vision pass a *join* — ship the crops, get codes back, fill the column — rather than a re-parse of everything. Designing it in now costs one column; retrofitting it later would mean re-running the whole extraction. **Measured 2026-08-06, and it breaks that plan: the slots are not all the markers.** Over the 20-page pilot the text layer emits **291** unresolved slots where the image reads find **893** printed symbols (glm-ocr) and **545** (qwen3.5) — a threefold undercount, with only 16 of 221 municipality entries agreeing exactly and 185 holding more symbols than the ALTO saw. The cause is visible in :data:`_GLYPH_RE`, which can only recognise a marker that OCR'd into something that is *not* a letter. A pictogram the engine rendered as ``Щ``, ``ф`` or ``$`` becomes a slot; the same pictogram rendered as ``g``, ``f``, ``p`` or ``S`` — which is the commoner outcome — is indistinguishable from type and is never emitted at all. Page 270 prints four symbols in ``1, 1) [school] II, [doctor], [fire-brigade], [cooperative]: R``; the ALTO gives ``g II, $, f, R.`` and yields **one** slot. So "the text layer knows where every marker is, the image read knows what it is" is false, and which third it knows is decided by how the OCR happened to fail. :func:`join_symbols` can still fill a slot, but its count guard cannot be a gate: the two channels are not counting the same thing, so a disagreement is the normal case and not evidence about the reader. For the offices sections the image read has to be the *primary* record and this module's slots a lower bound — which moves the burden of proof onto two independent readers agreeing (:func:`compare_passes`) rather than onto agreement with the ALTO. Two cautions that come from the source rather than from the code: * **The two editions disagree on letters.** A building cooperative is ``St`` in the Czech volume and ``B`` in the German. Never join the editions on the letter. * **The language suffix is the point and it does not survive.** ``Hč`` versus ``Hn`` marks a cooperative as Czech or German — an ethnic-institutional variable with no equivalent in the census — and the OCR keeps it on 2 occurrences in 188. It is recorded as ``language_suffix`` where present and left empty otherwise, never guessed. A block matching no obec in its okres is a settlement row wrongly promoted; an obec with no block is a municipality the parser lost. Neither is visible to any arithmetic identity. A canonical identity for the output — okres_id plus the modern Czech name — which the final dataset needs regardless. The German names are the hard part. settlements_1910 carries de_name for only 18% of Bohemian obce and name_1910 for 33%. Two further sources close most of the gap: settlement_aliases_1910.csv — 10,028 "viz" cross-references from the ČSÚ historical lexicon, most of them German forms pointing at a Czech target. The Czech volume itself. It prints every municipality bilingually — "Bílek, Bilek", "Štěpánov, Stěpanow", "Bobkov, také Doubkov, Dobkau" — so once a Czech block is anchored, the German half of its own name cell becomes a variant of that obec. The source we are parsing is the best-covered crosswalk available for it, which is why anchoring runs in two passes: Czech first, harvest, then German. Columns 16 and 17 of the table print *keys* — ``13)``, ``10) 2 1/4`` — that point into a block beneath the table body. Until now that block was outside the extraction entirely: :func:`~utils.lexikon_1910.lexikon_1910.body_band` deliberately ends where the shortest column rule stops, so the pipeline transcribed pointers into a legend it never read. The block is found the same way the table is — from the printed rules, not from the text. A short vertical rule starts where the body rules stop and splits the footnote into two columns; its own extent gives the band and its x position gives the split. **It is a column flow, not a two-part layout.** The text runs down the left column and continues at the top of the right, newspaper-fashion, and within that flow two kinds of section alternate, each introduced by its own heading: ``Části osad v soudním okresu X`` the parts each settlement is made of, each with a house–population pair ``Úřady, ústavy a t. d. v soudním okresu X`` post office, telegraph, parish, school, railway station and altitude, keyed by the numbers the table references So a section is *not* a column: one page carries the tail of one district's offices and the head of the next district's parts, and both may straddle the divider. Sections are therefore cut on their headings in reading order, which also recovers the thing that makes the key check work — **the district each key set belongs to.** The numbering restarts in every soudní okres, so a key set pooled across districts would resolve almost any reference and check nothing. **What is recoverable here is much less than what is printed, and the difference is the point.** The offices sections are mostly *pictograms* — a post horn, a bell, a telegraph key — which carry the meaning and which the OCR renders as ``Щ1``, ``gg§!``, ``ф``, ``ľ``. No amount of parsing recovers a symbol the engine never saw. This module extracts the three things that survive as text — the key numbers, the altitudes in metres, and the house–population pairs — and reports the rest as unrecovered rather than guessing at it. What the key numbers are good for is a closed-set check. Within one soudní okres they run 1..N, so a key referenced from the table that is not in the set is an OCR error with a short candidate list. That is how ``,3)`` is recoverable as ``13)``: 13 is in the set and ``,3`` is not. The first was built around one measured number — Opus over every table block ≈ $432 — and that number pushed the whole design toward free local readers: Ollama, tight crops, a billed channel off by default. Those readers did not get there. The 2026-08-14 bake-off settled at F1 0.693 with 29.8 % of municipalities read exactly right , and the follow-up measurement showed the adjudication band that would have to be closed by hand is 5.5–7.0 claims per entry — ~44,000–56,000 decisions over the volume, touching 93 % of entries . That is a third to two-thirds of the cost of simply hand-transcribing the apparatus, so no amount of adjudication rescues the architecture. Two things changed, and together they invert the design. The cost constraint dissolved. The $432 was for the table, which nobody reads with a model. Priced against the job actually being done — one call per page — the whole Čechy + Böhmen run on batch rates is $32 on Gemini 3.8 Flash and $54 on Haiku 4.5 . The entire model range fits inside a hundred dollars, so the reader is chosen on accuracy and nothing else. Resolution was never actually tested. render_page renders to the ALTO frame width, 2,714 px, so a CZ page is 2,714 × 3,976. The Anthropic vision API downscales any image whose long edge exceeds ~1568 px, which puts a whole page at 0.37× native and the crops the entire bake-off ran on at 0.58× . At 0.58× an entry line is 25 px tall and a [school] pictogram is about 29 × 12 px. The human read them at 44 px and 50 × 21 and reported zero illegible glyphs. So the readers have never once been shown the marks at the size the paper prints them. The bake-off varied crop height (halving — lost for all four models) and upscaling (a wash); it never varied the thing that decides what the model sees. Hence the unit here: one page record, assembled from native-resolution tiles , never one downscaled page image. What is deliberately unchanged The gold sample design, the calibration/certification split, the closed symbol vocabulary, and the grader. Claims are emitted in exactly the columns inventory_*.csv already uses, so utils.lexikon_1910.lexikon_1910_institutions.score_against_reference and every bake-off comparison consume this module's output with no new code. A v2 that needed a new grader would not be comparable to v1, and the comparison is the point. Three switches, no edits RunConfig carries models / mode / transport / editions / geometries . MODELS is a registry: one entry per model holding the provider, price, batch discount, image-tokenizer rule and thinking policy. Adding a model is one entry; selecting one is a string in a list. Provider SDKs import lazily inside their adapter , so a Gemini-only run never imports anthropic and nothing breaks when only one SDK is installed. This is the second generation of the register digitisation. The first was built around one measured number — Opus over every *table block* ≈ $432 — and that number pushed the whole design toward free local readers: Ollama, tight crops, a billed channel off by default. Those readers did not get there. The 2026-08-14 bake-off settled at **F1 0.693** with **29.8 % of municipalities read exactly right**, and the follow-up measurement showed the adjudication band that would have to be closed by hand is **5.5–7.0 claims per entry** — ~44,000–56,000 decisions over the volume, touching **93 % of entries**. That is a third to two-thirds of the cost of simply hand-transcribing the apparatus, so no amount of adjudication rescues the architecture. Two things changed, and together they invert the design. **The cost constraint dissolved.** The $432 was for the table, which nobody reads with a model. Priced against the job actually being done — one call per page — the whole Čechy + Böhmen run on batch rates is **$32 on Gemini 3.8 Flash** and **$54 on Haiku 4.5**. The entire model range fits inside a hundred dollars, so the reader is chosen on accuracy and nothing else. **Resolution was never actually tested.** ``render_page`` renders to the ALTO frame width, 2,714 px, so a CZ page is 2,714 × 3,976. The Anthropic vision API downscales any image whose long edge exceeds ~1568 px, which puts a whole page at **0.37× native** and the crops the entire bake-off ran on at **0.58×**. At 0.58× an entry line is 25 px tall and a ``[school]`` pictogram is about 29 × 12 px. The human read them at 44 px and 50 × 21 and reported *zero* illegible glyphs. So the readers have never once been shown the marks at the size the paper prints them. The bake-off varied crop *height* (halving — lost for all four models) and upscaling (a wash); it never varied the thing that decides what the model sees. Hence the unit here: **one page record, assembled from native-resolution tiles**, never one downscaled page image. What is deliberately unchanged ------------------------------ The gold sample design, the calibration/certification split, the closed symbol vocabulary, and the grader. Claims are emitted in **exactly** the columns ``inventory_*.csv`` already uses, so :func:`~utils.lexikon_1910.lexikon_1910_institutions.score_against_reference` and every bake-off comparison consume this module's output with no new code. A v2 that needed a new grader would not be comparable to v1, and the comparison is the point. Three switches, no edits ------------------------ :class:`RunConfig` carries ``models`` / ``mode`` / ``transport`` / ``editions`` / ``geometries``. :data:`MODELS` is a registry: one entry per model holding the provider, price, batch discount, image-tokenizer rule and thinking policy. Adding a model is one entry; selecting one is a string in a list. Provider SDKs import **lazily inside their adapter**, so a Gemini-only run never imports ``anthropic`` and nothing breaks when only one SDK is installed. Because the tokenizer rule lives on the spec, the tiler is model-aware: Gemini takes the page whole at native resolution (its 768 px crops handle it, at ~3× fewer tokens), Anthropic gets ten native tiles. The table above it is digits between printed rules and the ALTO reads it at ~88 %; the apparatus is small type, superscript keys, and — for most of what it records — pictograms , which the OCR renders as Щ1 , gg§! , ф , ľ . Those are not damaged characters that better parsing recovers. The engine never identified a symbol, so there is nothing in the text layer to parse, and utils.lexikon_1910.lexikon_1910_institutions correctly emits them as unresolved slots rather than guessing. This module fills those slots by looking at the paper. It is deliberately the narrowest possible vision channel: One call per region, not per municipality. The apparatus is three crops on a page (left column, right column, the full-width postal footer). The table above it is ~15 blocks. Reading the apparatus for the whole Čechy volume is therefore on the order of 2,300 calls against ~11,775 for the table — which is what makes a cheap reader on the apparatus and no reader on the table an affordable combination. It returns printed lines, not structure. The reply is a list of strings in printed order, which is exactly what utils.lexikon_1910.lexikon_1910_notes.extract_notes produces from the ALTO. So a vision read is assembled straight into a utils.lexikon_1910.lexikon_1910_notes.Notes and every downstream consumer — section cutting, parts_check , the postal legend, the institution decoder — runs on it without a line of new code , and the two channels are gradeable against each other because they produce the same object. Symbols come back as tokens from a closed list. The model may emit [post] , [school] , [doctor] … and nothing else; anything it cannot place is [?] . The vocabulary is not invented here — it is the pictogram rows of reference/places/institution_abbreviations.csv , so the decoder resolves a token by the same table lookup it uses for o. hjtm. or gymn. , and a token outside the table is rejected on arrival rather than becoming an institution nobody curated. The closed set is doing the same job the invariants do for the table. There is no arithmetic identity down here to catch a confabulated symbol, so the only defence is that the model cannot name anything that is not on the list, and that an unknown symbol has a place to go — [?] — that is not a wrong answer. A vocabulary the model can extend at will would produce a clean-looking inventory with no way to tell which parts of it were read and which were composed. The symbol legend itself is provisional until the preface plates (pp. VIII–XIV) are transcribed; the tokens carry that in their note column. Getting the vocabulary wrong misnames an institution — it does not silently invent one — and the fix is a CSV edit plus a re-run of these crops, not a re-extraction. What changes from volume to volume is small and enumerable, and this module is where it is written down rather than scattered through the parsers: the source — which PDF, whether it carries an ALTO, a word layer, plain text, or nothing; the scans that are table pages, and which are the statutory cities' prose pages; the language of the headings — Části osad v soudním okresu X: against Ortsbestandteile im Gerichtsbezirk X: — and of the abbreviations; the column schema — Silesia prints a fourth Umgangssprache column ( polnisch ), so its table has 18 columns and its language identity four parts. A crown-land volume not yet owned (Galicia, Bukovina, the Littoral) will differ in exactly this place. A profile is a TOML file under reference/places/volumes/<slug>.toml , read with the standard library's tomllib (Python 3.11+). Nothing in the existing pipeline reads a profile. lexikon_1910 , lexikon_1910_notes and the pilot keep their own constants, which are the Czech volume's; czech_drift checks that the Czech profile states exactly those constants, so the two cannot diverge unnoticed, and the image-only geometry ( lexikon_1910_image ) and its measurement scripts are the code that takes a profile. Moving the module constants themselves onto the profile is a mechanical follow-up that would make every import depend on tomllib ; it is left for the author to decide. This module finds the boxes on the gold section images ( transcription_gold/cz/{calibration,purposive} ) in three steps: Candidates. The ink is split into connected components, each component is put on its printed line, small marks at the foot of the line (full stops, commas) are set aside, and the rest are joined left to right into clusters wherever the gap is narrower than a word space. A cluster is a word, a number, a key — or a glyph. Every cluster gets shape features in line heights: width, height, ink density, holes, stroke width, where it sits against the baseline. Glyphness. A logistic model on those features says how much a cluster looks like a pictogram rather than type. It is trained without a single hand label: the gold says how many marks each entry prints and in what order, the alignment below picks that many clusters, and the clusters it picks are the positives of the next round ( train_glyphness ). Only calibration pages train it (D-69), and a calibration page is scored by a model that never saw it. Alignment. The clusters of a section, in reading order, are matched to the claims, in printed order (D-73: the order of the marks is a fact of the print, and the order check in the scorer already relies on it). A monotone dynamic programme picks one cluster per claim, maximising the summed score, may leave a claim unplaced at a cost, and keeps every claim inside its own entry's lines where the entries can be located. The score of cluster i for claim j is a matrix, so the encoder's similarity to the claimed token's exemplars ( run_glyph_e3.py ) is added on Heavyhorse6 without touching this code. Modifiers (1.1.0). The plate builds a fifth of its tokens from another: (school) is [school-exp] , ♁ A is [ev-parish-ab] , (block of four) is [colony] ( glyph_composites.csv ). A claim is therefore placed on its base glyph — templates and sizes are kept per base — and brackets are never part of a cluster nor the base of a claim. Beside each placed base the brackets (round or square) and a letter are then looked for without the claim ( modifiers ), so the check of a claim cannot be steered by it. The claims can be the gold's (to measure the locator, and to cut the bank) or a reader's (to check that reader): the boxes then show the encoder what the reader says is there. A glyph no claim mentions is not placed — which is why the glyphness score is also written for every cluster, for a later pass that looks for marks nobody read. measure scores the locator against the 141 glyphs the author clicked for test A ( output/glyph_bank/glyph_bank.csv ): the share of clicked glyphs inside some candidate, inside the box aligned to their claim, the centre distance, and the clusters per entry that look like glyphs but carry no claim. python utils/lexikon_1910/locate_glyphs.py # train, align, measure python utils/lexikon_1910/locate_glyphs.py --draw 0136 # + overlays for a scan Certification sheets are refused ( ROLES ); nothing here reads them. Nothing in the pipeline says *where* a mark is: the readers return tokens, and test A (D-91) showed that on a clean box even 32 x 32 pixels tell the fill pairs apart — so the box is the hard part. This module finds the boxes on the gold section images (``transcription_gold/cz/{calibration,purposive}``) in three steps: 1. **Candidates.** The ink is split into connected components, each component is put on its printed line, small marks at the foot of the line (full stops, commas) are set aside, and the rest are joined left to right into clusters wherever the gap is narrower than a word space. A cluster is a word, a number, a key — or a glyph. Every cluster gets shape features in line heights: width, height, ink density, holes, stroke width, where it sits against the baseline. 2. **Glyphness.** A logistic model on those features says how much a cluster looks like a pictogram rather than type. It is trained without a single hand label: the gold says how many marks each entry prints and in what order, the alignment below picks that many clusters, and the clusters it picks are the positives of the next round (``train_glyphness``). Only calibration pages train it (D-69), and a calibration page is scored by a model that never saw it. 3. **Alignment.** The clusters of a section, in reading order, are matched to the claims, in printed order (D-73: the order of the marks is a fact of the print, and the order check in the scorer already relies on it). A monotone dynamic programme picks one cluster per claim, maximising the summed score, may leave a claim unplaced at a cost, and keeps every claim inside its own entry's lines where the entries can be located. The score of cluster *i* for claim *j* is a matrix, so the encoder's similarity to the claimed token's exemplars (``run_glyph_e3.py``) is added on Heavyhorse6 without touching this code. 4. **Modifiers** (1.1.0). The plate builds a fifth of its tokens from another: ``(school)`` is ``[school-exp]``, ``♁ A`` is ``[ev-parish-ab]``, ``(block of four)`` is ``[colony]`` (``glyph_composites.csv``). A claim is therefore placed on its **base** glyph — templates and sizes are kept per base — and brackets are never part of a cluster nor the base of a claim. Beside each placed base the brackets (round or square) and a letter are then looked for **without the claim** (:func:`modifiers`), so the check of a claim cannot be steered by it. The claims can be the gold's (to measure the locator, and to cut the bank) or a reader's (to check that reader): the boxes then show the encoder what the reader says is there. A glyph no claim mentions is not placed — which is why the glyphness score is also written for every cluster, for a later pass that looks for marks nobody read. ``measure`` scores the locator against the 141 glyphs the author clicked for test A (``output/glyph_bank/glyph_bank.csv``): the share of clicked glyphs inside some candidate, inside the box aligned to their claim, the centre distance, and the clusters per entry that look like glyphs but carry no claim. python utils/lexikon_1910/locate_glyphs.py # train, align, measure python utils/lexikon_1910/locate_glyphs.py --draw 0136 # + overlays for a scan Certification sheets are refused (``ROLES``); nothing here reads them. TL;DR Build the gold worksheets for the German edition (Spezialortsrepertorium Böhmen). 1910 register · v1.1.0 · 271 lines · 5 public functions · 15 constants · used by nothing else · utils/lexikon_1910/make_gold_worksheet_de.py load_manifest render sheet_text build main ROOT DE_PDF MANIFEST OUT_ROOT RESOLUTION ENLARGE UPPER_BAND LOWER_BAND LEDGER_LINES BLANK_KEY MD_HEADER SCOPE_COURT VOLUMES VOLUME_ROWS TWIN How it works Companion to make_gold_worksheet , which builds the Czech sheets and is left alone. The German sheet has the same four sections and the same block grammar — pipe rows for the table, ledger fences for the two-column part, a legend and a notes fence — so read_transcription_md can cut it into the same blocks. Three things differ, and each follows from the source: Nothing is pre-filled, the ledger keys included. The Czech sheet takes its municipality names and row counts from the ALTO text layer. The UBW scan has no ALTO and its embedded text is too damaged to print beside a blank cell ( NiederalteDbuch , Altniynitz ), so the transcriber types the key and the names as printed. An unfilled ledger line keeps the Czech sheets' __,+ template key, which the reader counts as blank and never as an entry. The images are the page, not its sections. Without coordinates there is no section to cut, so each scan is rendered whole, plus an upper and a lower band that overlap, enlarged like the Czech crops. The pages come from a manifest, not from a draw. A German page is not the twin of a Czech page: each edition orders a district's municipalities alphabetically in its own language. gold_sample_pages_de.csv names each German scan, the Czech scans it shares municipalities with, and whether the whole page is read or only one court's part of it. The district in every heading is the Czech court name ( soudní okres Trutnov ), because that is the half of the join key the Czech gold already carries. The municipality number is not shared between the editions, so the two golds join on names, never on muni_seq . A sheet that exists is never overwritten: it may hold an hour of reading. python utils/lexikon_1910/make_gold_worksheet_de.py --role purposive python utils/lexikon_1910/make_gold_worksheet_de.py --role purposive --images python utils/lexikon_1910/make_gold_worksheet_de.py --volume maehren_de --role certification --volume (1.1.0, D-133) cuts the sheets of Moravia's or Silesia's own drawn sample ( gold_sample_pages_<slug>.csv , from draw_gold_sample.py --volume ) into transcription_gold/de-moravia/ or de-silesia/ . Those pages have no Czech twin and no court is pre-filled: the court and every name are typed from the print. That sheet asked for one of the three documents the register prints; this one asks for all of them, so it needs its own reader — and the two must both keep working, because the four purposive pages are transcribed under both protocols and the disagreement between them is a measurement of the transcriber that nothing else in this project can make. What it emits ------------- Four frames, from the four sections of a ``<scan>.md`` sheet: ``inventory_human.csv`` section 2b, in **exactly** the columns the model passes produce, so ``score_against_reference`` and the bake-off's comparisons consume it unchanged ``parts_human.csv`` section 2a — the named parts, their topographic mark and their house–population pair ``table_human.csv`` section 1 — the seventeen columns, one row per printed line ``legend_human.csv`` section 3 — the postal and station keys Why it grades as it reads ------------------------- **The register's own arithmetic is a check on the person, not only on the OCR.** The table has to add up four ways and the ``Části osad`` pairs have to sum to the settlement's row above them, and none of that was available while the sheet asked only for symbols: the apparatus has no arithmetic, so a symbols-only gold could be graded by nothing but a second reading of the same pages. Batched, each reader costs half, and the route does not care how a reply arrived — only that the crop cache holds it. So: prepare — the pilot runs with --batch-prepare QUEUE : every crop not in its cache becomes one line of QUEUE (the cache key, the cache folder and the request the reader would have sent), and nothing is sent; submit ( submit ) — Claude lines go to the Message Batches API; Gemini lines, once GEMINI_BATCH is on, to Gemini's native Batch API (1.4.0): each request translated by to_native , written into JSONL input files under the File API's limit, uploaded, one job a file; collect ( collect ) — each reply is parsed as the reader parses a live one and written into the crop cache under its key, in the pilot's own format; the pilot runs again without the flag and finds every crop in its cache. A reply that fails — an error, a truncation, a setting the batch endpoint refuses — is not cached: the second run reads that crop live, as before. So the worst a batch can do is cost a little and save nothing; it cannot lose a crop. State lives beside the queue ( <queue>.batches.json ). A queue line may carry payload_key — "rows" for a table block (1.1.0) — which names the reply's list as the reader names it; the cache record keeps it under lines either way, as both the notes' and the table's caches read it. Gemini, natively (1.4.0, D-117). The OpenAI-compatible batch endpoint refused the structured output the live reader sends, so Gemini's lines now go to the native Batch API in Gemini's own dialect. That is the measured reader only if the translation is exact: to_native maps every field it knows and refuses every other, and each line is checked against its live request before it is written ( _same_request ; check_translation runs that over a whole queue, offline). Whether the replies are the measured reader's is then measured, not assumed: gemini_equivalence_submit and gemini_equivalence_collect send gold requests that already have live readings through the native path into a scratch folder, and hold the replies to a bar written before anything is sent ( EQUIVALENCE_BAR ). GEMINI_BATCH stays off until that check passes on the machine of record. A line at a time (1.4.0). A volume's queue runs to ~12 GB for Gemini and ~17 GB for each Haiku pass. index_queue keeps each line's envelope and where it starts; a request is loaded only while its batch is written, and collect reads the queue only once a batch has ended — a poll while every batch is processing reads nothing. This script applies lexikon_1910_institutions 0.6.0 to the inventories already on disk and writes all four. It reads inventory_human.csv and every inventory_<label>.csv under output/lexikon_1910_pilot/bakeoff/<host>/ . The inventories are the decoded passes, so nothing is re-decoded here: a pass written before the 0.5.0 decoder fix still carries its misfiled parts, and its row says so in false_misfiled . Rate-limited passes are excluded, as everywhere ( bakeoff.passes_on_disk ). What it does not cover: the whole-page (v2) repeats of 2026-09-10, which are rebuilt from raw payloads by run_e1_gemini_version.py and whose pipeline the plan has stopped. Outputs, all under output/lexikon_1910_pilot/bakeoff/ , named for the run tag ( r4 here) so an earlier run's report is not overwritten by a later one: rescore_r4_accuracy.csv one row per pass: both units, counts, interval rescore_r4_symbol_rates.csv one row per (pass, glyph): tp fp fn tn, rates rescore_r4_part_attribution.csv one row per misfiled institution rescore_r4_named_parts.csv one row per pass: the Části osad parts rescore_r4_parts_symbols.csv one row per named part whose symbol differs rescore_r4_attributes.csv one row per (pass, attribute): schools, burgher schools, cooperatives rescore_r4_order.csv one row per pass: what the printed order of the marks flags (I22) rescore_r4_order_flags.csv one row per flagged mark, on every page rescore_r4_order_disputes.csv one row per pair of passes: the flags on the claims the two disagree on rescore_r4_report.txt the ledgers below, as printed The last three need the two files a pass writes since 2026-10-06 — its named parts ( parts_<label>.csv ) and what it read beside the school and cooperative glyphs ( attributes_<label>.csv ) — and the gold's own, parts_human.csv and attributes_human.csv . A pass read before that date has neither until it is replayed from its crop cache; it is then scored on symbols only, and says so. The three order files are the printed-order check of lexikon_1910_institutions 0.9.0 (D-73). It needs each mark's place in its line, which an inventory does not keep, so it reads the pass's decoded records, institutions_<label>.csv . The order itself is learned from the gold sheets of the purposive and calibration roles, read directly ( read_transcription_md.read_order_reference ) and never from the sealed certification sheets; each page is judged on the order of the other pages. The check flags and routes. It changes no claim, and no figure above it moves. TL;DR E1 — is the gap between the two cloud pipelines the model, or the view? 1910 register · v1.2.1 · 638 lines · 17 public functions · 16 constants · used by utils/lexikon_1910/run_e1b_second_reader.py , utils/lexikon_1910/run_frozen.py , utils/lexikon_1910/run_r5_german_notes.py +1 · utils/lexikon_1910/run_e1_gemini_version.py label plan flags seed_first_repeat quota_open wait_for_quota cache_usage input_tokens run load_csv v2_claims per_entry pooled majority glyph_errors score main HERE ROOT REPEATS VARIANT KIND WORKERS MODELS SEED V2_RAW V2_RUNS E1_RUN_TAG OUT_CSV OUT_REPORT GEMINI_URL ARM GEOMETRY_ARM How it works SYMBOL_ACCURACY_PLAN.md (revision of 2026-09-17) records a ladder: Gemini 3.7 Flash on the bake-off's section crops reads the 280-claim gold at F1 0.964, and Gemini 3.8 Flash on whole pages (notebook 06) at 0.845 at best. The last step of that ladder changes three things at once — the model version, the size of what one call is shown, and the job the call is given — so it cannot say which one paid. This experiment holds the crops, the prompt, the atlas and every flag fixed and changes only the model : arm A gemini-3.7-flash on the bake-off crops 3 repeats arm B gemini-3.8-flash on the bake-off crops 3 repeats arm C gemini-3.8-flash whole-page halfbands the 5 repeats of 2026-09-10 arm D gemini-3.7-flash on the bake-off crops 3 repeats, thinking OFF arm E gemini-3.8-flash on the bake-off crops 3 repeats, thinking OFF A − B is the version effect; B − C is what the view and the task cost. Arms D and E (added 2026-09-22) switch Gemini's thinking off with reasoning_effort="none" : A − D and B − E are what thinking buys on the crops, and E − C compares crops with whole pages with thinking off on both sides — the cleaner version of B − C. Repeats are not optional here: Gemini is not deterministic (five halfbands repeats span F1 0.804–0.878), so one run per arm would compare two draws, not two readers. What is held fixed, and how that is known The flags are bakeoff.flags_for for the atlas variant of the gold kind — 13 pages, both apparatus documents, strips of 500 px, upscaled, atlas on, temperature 0 — with the reader switched from the Ollama daemon to the hosted endpoint. That this reproduces the 2026-08-30 pass exactly was checked, not assumed : re-running gemini37_r3atlasg with these flags against a copy of its crop cache served 81 of 81 crops from cache, and the cache key hashes the crop bytes, the caption, the model, the system prompt, the temperature and the atlas. Arm A's first repeat is that 2026-08-30 reading, re-decoded by today's code : its cache is copied under the new label, so no request is made and the answers are the model's own. Re-decoding matters — the stored inventory scores F1 0.964 and the same answers decoded today score 0.975, because the decoder changed after the pass was written. Every pass in this experiment is decoded by the same code. Arms A and B send no thinking setting, so each runs on its provider default — which on Gemini 3.x Flash is thousands of thinking tokens a crop, billed as output and, before 2026-09-22, never booked by the pilot (see SYMBOL_ACCURACY_PLAN.md , Correction ). Arm C was run with thinking explicitly off, and so are D and E. Scoring score_against_reference against inventory_human.csv (4 purposive pages; 47 entries and 280 claims when E1 ran, 61 and 372 since D-65 — the report prints what the file holds): P / R / F1 / entry_exact per repeat, the mean and range per arm, a ≥ 2-of-3 majority per arm, the claims each arm gets wrong by glyph, and a bootstrap over entries for the two differences. The bootstrap treats the 47 entries as independent; they sit on four pages, so its intervals are too narrow and are reported as a lower bound on the uncertainty. Usage python utils/lexikon_1910/run_e1_gemini_version.py # run what is missing, then score python utils/lexikon_1910/run_e1_gemini_version.py --arm off # only the thinking-off arms python utils/lexikon_1910/run_e1_gemini_version.py --wait 120 # first poll up to 120 min for quota python utils/lexikon_1910/run_e1_gemini_version.py --score # score only, spend nothing python utils/lexikon_1910/run_e1_gemini_version.py --dry-run # print the plan and the flags A pass whose inventory exists is skipped. The quota is asked before every pass that needs the network, and a refused request (HTTP 429) mid-pass parks it exactly as bakeoff does. Either way the runner does not push on — the quota belongs to the account, so every later pass would be refused too. Without --wait it stops; with it, it goes back to waiting for whatever time is left, and it counts the quota as open only after two consecutive requests are answered. Repeats are not optional here: Gemini is not deterministic (five `halfbands` repeats span F1 0.804–0.878), so one run per arm would compare two draws, not two readers. What is held fixed, and how that is known ------------------------------------------ The flags are :func:`bakeoff.flags_for` for the `atlas` variant of the `gold` kind — 13 pages, both apparatus documents, strips of 500 px, upscaled, atlas on, temperature 0 — with the reader switched from the Ollama daemon to the hosted endpoint. That this reproduces the 2026-08-30 pass exactly was **checked, not assumed**: re-running `gemini37_r3atlasg` with these flags against a copy of its crop cache served **81 of 81** crops from cache, and the cache key hashes the crop bytes, the caption, the model, the system prompt, the temperature and the atlas. Arm A's first repeat is that 2026-08-30 reading, **re-decoded by today's code**: its cache is copied under the new label, so no request is made and the answers are the model's own. Re-decoding matters — the stored inventory scores F1 0.964 and the same answers decoded today score 0.975, because the decoder changed after the pass was written. Every pass in this experiment is decoded by the same code. Arms A and B send no thinking setting, so each runs on its provider default — which on Gemini 3.x Flash is thousands of thinking tokens a crop, billed as output and, before 2026-09-22, never booked by the pilot (see ``SYMBOL_ACCURACY_PLAN.md``, *Correction*). Arm C was run with thinking explicitly off, and so are D and E. Opus cannot be that reader over a whole volume, on cost. This screen chooses a cheap one, and it does not choose on accuracy alone: a second reader is worth what it brings to review — the first reader's errors it disagrees on, less the alarms it raises on claims the first reader had right (`lexikon_1910_institutions.second_reader`). Two readers at 0.97 that make the same mistakes are one reader read twice, and the r4 baseline says that is what a second Gemini pass is: its substitutions (castle / poorhouse, ruin / solitary house, myslivna / hájovna ) recur in every repeat and in both versions. So the bar a candidate has to clear is on disk before anything is spent — --score prints it. What is held fixed Everything the reader is shown. The flags are bakeoff.flags_for for the atlas variant of the gold kind, exactly as E1 and the r4 baseline sent them — 13 pages, both apparatus documents, strips of 500 px, upscaled, atlas on, temperature 0 — and only the transport changes. The crops are therefore the 81 the baseline read. The candidates CANDIDATES . The two that run by default need no new account: Claude Haiku 4.5, on the Anthropic key already in .secrets/api_keys.json , and qwen3.8:27b on the local Ollama daemon, which is free. One pass each; a finalist gets three ( --repeats 3 --candidates haiku45 ). Claude Haiku 5.5 (2026-10-08) is on file twice, on the same key, and off by default: haiku55 with thinking asked off, as the default reader's is, and haiku55t as the model runs unasked, with adaptive thinking. The first table of --score sets either beside gemini38 as a reader in its own right, which is the comparison to make before asking what it adds as a second one. Two further arms, haiku55n and haiku55nh , send the thinking arm the prompt's note for a reader that thinks, at medium and at high effort. Three more are on file and off by default, because they need an OpenRouter account and its key ( OPENROUTER_API_KEY ): Qwen3-VL, MiniMax M3 and Kimi K2.5. They are the next thing to try only if neither default clears the bar. Their ids and prices were read off OpenRouter's own model list on 2026-10-06 and are checked against it again before each such pass (the list is public and costs nothing): an id that is gone skips its candidate, a price that moved is printed. --list shows what that endpoint offers today. Before a hosted pass, one tiny request is sent as the pass would send it — same model, same settings. A model or a parameter the endpoint refuses is then found by one request instead of by eighty-one crops. somewhere else than Gemini? ``SYMBOL_ACCURACY_PLAN.md`` keeps Gemini Flash as the reader of record and asks for a second reader that **routes and never overwrites** (D-38, D-55): a claim the two agree on is accepted, a claim only one makes goes to review. Opus cannot be that reader over a whole volume, on cost. This screen chooses a cheap one, and it does not choose on accuracy alone: a second reader is worth what it brings to review — the first reader's errors it disagrees on, less the alarms it raises on claims the first reader had right (``lexikon_1910_institutions.second_reader``). Two readers at 0.97 that make the same mistakes are one reader read twice, and the r4 baseline says that is what a second Gemini pass is: its substitutions (castle / poorhouse, ruin / solitary house, *myslivna* / *hájovna*) recur in every repeat and in both versions. So the bar a candidate has to clear is on disk before anything is spent — ``--score`` prints it. What is held fixed ------------------ Everything the reader is shown. The flags are :func:`bakeoff.flags_for` for the `atlas` variant of the `gold` kind, exactly as E1 and the r4 baseline sent them — 13 pages, both apparatus documents, strips of 500 px, upscaled, atlas on, temperature 0 — and only the transport changes. The crops are therefore the 81 the baseline read. The candidates -------------- :data:`CANDIDATES`. **The two that run by default need no new account:** Claude Haiku 4.5, on the Anthropic key already in ``.secrets/api_keys.json``, and qwen3.8:27b on the local Ollama daemon, which is free. One pass each; a finalist gets three (``--repeats 3 --candidates haiku45``). **Claude Haiku 5.5** (2026-10-08) is on file twice, on the same key, and off by default: ``haiku55`` with thinking asked off, as the default reader's is, and ``haiku55t`` as the model runs unasked, with adaptive thinking. The first table of ``--score`` sets either beside ``gemini38`` as a reader in its own right, which is the comparison to make before asking what it adds as a second one. Two further arms, ``haiku55n`` and ``haiku55nh``, send the thinking arm the prompt's note for a reader that thinks, at medium and at high effort. Three more are on file and off by default, because they need an OpenRouter account and its key (``OPENROUTER_API_KEY``): Qwen3-VL, MiniMax M3 and Kimi K2.5. They are the next thing to try only if neither default clears the bar. Their ids and prices were read off OpenRouter's own model list on 2026-10-06 and are checked against it again before each such pass (the list is public and costs nothing): an id that is gone skips its candidate, a price that moved is printed. ``--list`` shows what that endpoint offers today. Before a hosted pass, one tiny request is sent **as the pass would send it** — same model, same settings. A model or a parameter the endpoint refuses is then found by one request instead of by eighty-one crops. script-utils-lexikon_1910-run_e3_pages: TL;DR E3 on any page: the locator and DINOv3 on the readers' saved section crops (D-112). 1910 register · v0.1.0 · 280 lines · 8 public functions · 3 constants · used by 15_frozen_run.ipynb , utils/lexikon_1910/run_frozen.py · utils/lexikon_1910/run_e3_pages.py printed_munis sections_from_index full_locator full_detector Namer run rehearse main HERE ROOT VOLUME_ROLE How it works run_glyph_e3.py checks the readers on the gold pages: its sections come from the gold sheets, each page is placed by a locator trained on the other calibration pages, and each glyph is named against a bank that leaves its own page out. None of that exists for a page without a gold sheet. This runs the same check there: sections from the section crops the pilot saved ( section_images ), one per page, court and kind; the municipalities each prints, in order, from the readers' own output (any reader's row for the entry, with or without a mark); placement by one locator trained on every calibration page; the unclaimed-mark detector fitted on every calibration section, at the threshold the gold run set; naming against a bank of every gold glyph (calibration and purposive — the freeze, D-112), with one not in the bank threshold pooled over the gold. Its output has the columns of e3_verdicts_<tag>.csv ( gold blank), so the route and the ledger read it unchanged. Haiku's contrast sheet is the v1 layout (D-102, D-106), cut from calibration + purposive pages. read — Gemini 3.8 once, thinking off (the reader of record), Haiku 5.5 three times with the sheet (D-108); the Czech table by Gemini and Haiku once each (D-90). The reader of record's pass also saves every section crop it reads ( section_images.py ). With batch=True every reader — notes and table — is read in three steps: queue, batch, collect into its cache; a last pass reads them all from the cache ( reader_batches.py ). check — E3 on the saved crops ( run_e3_pages.py ): one locator, one detector and one bank taught by the whole gold; and the printed-order rule (D-73, D-74). On a German edition DINOv3 routes marks only if it passed the gate on the German gold ( e3_gate ). route — a part goes to Opus when its four readings do not all agree, or when they agree on a mark DINOv3 doubts or the order rule flags. One question per outlined mark, the whole entry in view (D-107), look-alike options (D-98), no whose-question (D-110), one call (D-111), batched and cached. opus — submit, then collect. A notebook run top to bottom waits at each collect until its batches have ended ( wait_for ), so it runs unattended. ledger — every mark's history and its final value (D-109); the marks Opus cannot tell go to the author's queue; the final inventory, each section's 1910 court beside its label ( courts.csv , lexikon_1910_courts , D-122); the place types ( final_types.csv , D-131) and the text abbreviations, counted ( final_abbreviations.csv , D-134). editions — Bohemia only, once both editions' final inventories exist: the Czech and German inventories compared municipality by municipality on the symbols both plates print, written beside them and into both ledgers as cz_de events ( compare_editions ); the German claims the Czech inventory disputes go to Opus on the German print ( anchor_claims , D-129). score — the gold only: the route's final value against the gold, beside the reader of record alone. The certification pages are scored once, apart. validation sample — a stratified random draw of marks by how each was settled, blind, with a separate key. review — the author's rulings and the validation sample as a Token Review queue ( review_queue ); the decisions come back as author events and validation answers ( apply_review ). EDITION = "bohemia" runs both editions of Bohemia in one pass through the notebook ( editions_for , 0.4.0): Czech first, since the German E3 gate is held to the Czech gold's E3, both read in the same batch window, and the two compared at the end. This script cuts each box from the gold section image, embeds it, and names it by the glyphs it is nearest to in a bank of labelled glyphs — a check that shares neither architecture nor training signal with the language-model readers. It routes a claim and never overwrites one (D-38, D-55, D-69): its output is a second opinion per mark, and a disagreement is a reason for a second look. The bank is the gold-placed glyphs of the calibration pages only (D-69), cut at printed size from entries, never from the legend plate. Each glyph is classified leave-page-out : a calibration page against the bank of the other seven, a purposive page against all eight. Reported for every encoder, cut and feature, 1-NN and 3-NN, per glyph type: accuracy over every gold mark the locator placed; a "not in the bank" answer : when the nearest neighbour is less similar than the threshold, the glyph is not named. The threshold for a page is the 5th percentile of the nearest-neighbour similarity of correctly named glyphs on the other calibration pages, so no page sets its own. A mark whose type the bank does not hold (a rare type printed on no other calibration page) should get it; a mark the bank does hold should not. A mark is named in parts (1.1.0). The first run named whole tokens on a window round the box, and the box held the base alone: [school-exp] came back [school] , [colony] [cottage-group] . Now the base is named on the base cut (the window with the brackets and letter the locator found beside it painted out) against a bank of bases — the bank's tokens taken apart, so a colony's block of four pools with [house-group] 's — the brackets by rule (both found: bracketed), the letter by 1-NN among the calibration pages' A / H crops, and only after a base the plate sets a letter after; then the token is composed from the plate's table. A combination the plate does not print, or a letter the bank cannot decide, is [not-in-legend] : routed, never forced. Reported beside the whole-token answer, per token, as before and after. Encoders. DINOv3 ViT-B/16 is the encoder of record (D-91); ViT-S/16 runs beside it; plain 32 x 32 pixels are the floor, and run anywhere. Weights load from the local Hugging Face cache only unless --download is given — this laptop has none, Heavyhorse6 has them ( notebooks/10_glyph_e3.ipynb ). Embeddings are saved ( embeddings_<encoder>_<cut>.npz ), so a later analysis need not re-run the encoder. Against the readers ( --tag , default r5 ). For every reader pass on disk under output/lexikon_1910_pilot/bakeoff/<host>/ (Czech passes only; rate-limited passes skipped), the reader's own claims — the offices symbols and the parts' topographic marks — are placed by the same locator on the same images, each placed box is named by the encoder, and the reader's token is set beside the encoder's and beside the gold mark whose box it falls on. Per pass, in the terms of D-71: the reader's errors the encoder disagrees with ( caught ), those it agrees with ( shared ), true claims it disagrees with ( alarms ), and how often the encoder is right when the two disagree. nearest neighbours on DINOv3 (D-69, D-72, D-93). ``locate_glyphs.py`` puts a box on every mark an entry is said to print. This script cuts each box from the gold section image, embeds it, and names it by the glyphs it is nearest to in a bank of labelled glyphs — a check that shares neither architecture nor training signal with the language-model readers. It **routes a claim and never overwrites one** (D-38, D-55, D-69): its output is a second opinion per mark, and a disagreement is a reason for a second look. **The bank** is the gold-placed glyphs of the **calibration** pages only (D-69), cut at printed size from entries, never from the legend plate. Each glyph is classified **leave-page-out**: a calibration page against the bank of the other seven, a purposive page against all eight. Reported for every encoder, cut and feature, 1-NN and 3-NN, per glyph type: * accuracy over every gold mark the locator placed; * a **"not in the bank" answer**: when the nearest neighbour is less similar than the threshold, the glyph is not named. The threshold for a page is the 5th percentile of the nearest-neighbour similarity of correctly named glyphs on the *other* calibration pages, so no page sets its own. A mark whose type the bank does not hold (a rare type printed on no other calibration page) should get it; a mark the bank does hold should not. **A mark is named in parts** (1.1.0). The first run named whole tokens on a window round the box, and the box held the base alone: ``[school-exp]`` came back ``[school]``, ``[colony]`` ``[cottage-group]``. Now the base is named on the ``base`` cut (the window with the brackets and letter the locator found beside it painted out) against a bank of bases — the bank's tokens taken apart, so a colony's block of four pools with ``[house-group]``'s — the brackets by rule (both found: bracketed), the letter by 1-NN among the calibration pages' A / H crops, and only after a base the plate sets a letter after; then the token is composed from the plate's table. A combination the plate does not print, or a letter the bank cannot decide, is ``[not-in-legend]``: routed, never forced. Reported beside the whole-token answer, per token, as before and after. **Encoders.** DINOv3 ViT-B/16 is the encoder of record (D-91); ViT-S/16 runs beside it; plain 32 x 32 pixels are the floor, and run anywhere. Weights load from the local Hugging Face cache only unless ``--download`` is given — this laptop has none, Heavyhorse6 has them (``notebooks/10_glyph_e3.ipynb``). Embeddings are saved (``embeddings_<encoder>_<cut>.npz``), so a later analysis need not re-run the encoder. **Against the readers** (``--tag``, default ``r5``). For every reader pass on disk under ``output/lexikon_1910_pilot/bakeoff/<host>/`` (Czech passes only; rate-limited passes skipped), the reader's own claims — the offices symbols and the parts' topographic marks — are placed by the same locator on the same images, each placed box is named by the encoder, and the reader's token is set beside the encoder's and beside the gold mark whose box it falls on. Per pass, in the terms of D-71: the reader's errors the encoder disagrees with (**caught**), those it agrees with (**shared**), true claims it disagrees with (**alarms**), and how often the encoder is right when the two disagree. The channels read the same pages without being told what the others said, and a deterministic grader that none of them can see scores the result: B the NDK ALTO text layer, snapped to the reconstructed grid (free) G the below-table apparatus, read from the image by an OCR model, returned as printed lines (billed, cheap) C the German volume, located by running head, both sides anchored to settlements_1910 and paired on the shared obec (free) A a vision model on a crop of a municipality block (billed, off by default) The spend is deliberately unequal, because the source is. Between the printed rules the ALTO reads digits at ~88%, and a second billed reading of a block that already satisfies every arithmetic identity buys confirmation of what was not in doubt. Below the rules it reads almost nothing worth having: the apparatus is small type, superscript keys, and — for most of what it records — pictograms , which no amount of parsing recovers from a text layer that never identified them. So the default run reads the apparatus with a model and the table without one. Channel A stays available for the blocks channel B failed ( --a-on-fail ), which is the only place a per-municipality rate is worth paying. The arithmetic is what makes that safe. The table has invariants; the apparatus has none, so its guard is a closed vocabulary : the reader may name a symbol only from the volume's own printed legend ( Výklad značek , p. XI, carried in institution_abbreviations.csv ), and anything else is [?] . A token off the list is rejected on arrival and counted in the ledger rather than normalised away. Channel G returns printed lines , not structure, so its output is assembled into the same Notes object the ALTO produces and every downstream consumer — section cutting, parts_check , the postal legend, the institution decoder — runs on it unchanged. That is what makes the two readings comparable instead of merely both present. Every block is also anchored against the municipalities its okres is known to contain. That is the only check here that can see a block which should not exist, or a municipality the parser lost — no arithmetic identity can. The readers are the only model-specific part: everything downstream (grid, blocks, invariants, anchoring, grader) is indifferent to which model produced the rows, so a candidate reader can be scored on exactly the same yardstick. The model never sees the invariants. It is asked to transcribe what is printed and nothing else — no mention that the sexes sum to the total, that the confessions sum to the total, or that the settlements sum to their municipality. A model told what the numbers must add up to will return numbers that add up, and the pass rate stops measuring anything. For the same reason a failing block is re-read, never repaired: nothing that fails is quietly patched into the output. Two local models, two different jobs Run against a local Ollama daemon, the reading costs nothing and the constraint becomes wall-clock. It is worth splitting the work by what each model is : A dedicated OCR model ( glm-ocr : 0.9B, of which the language side is a 0.5B decoder) transcribes this print better than a general model its size, and cannot be asked to hold an 83-token taxonomy or a JSON schema while doing it. It gets --notes-style transcribe and --notes-format text : every symbol comes back as [?] , which still records the position and the count of each one, so the slots survive for a later pass. A general vision-language model ( qwen3.5 , 4b/9b) can hold the closed list and the schema, so it gets --notes-style annotate and is the one that can actually name a post office or a school. Both defaults are inferred from the model id and announced. Run them as two labelled passes over the same pages and compare: the [?] slots from the first are exactly what the second has to fill, and both are graded against channel B by the same arithmetic. Why a section and not a column ( --notes-sections ) The two passes above want different crops, and it took a failure to see it. A footnote column is ~1,350 x 1,000 px of six-point type; glm-ocr reads it in one call, and qwen3.5 does not — on page 270 it returned the Části osad section and stopped, one line short of the Úřady heading and everything under it. Halving the column changed the failure mode rather than fixing it: the bottom halves came back well-formed and empty , which is worse, because a region with no lines reads downstream as a part of the page that was blank. So the crop is cut on the print instead. The register organises the apparatus into sections — one heading, one soudní okres, one kind — and the ALTO already knows where every heading sits, so --notes-sections offices sends each Úřady, ústavy section as its own image: a median of 478 px instead of a whole column, 1.77 crops a page instead of 3, a prompt that describes one kind of entry instead of five, and 56 symbol tokens instead of 83. What comes back is joined to the text layer's own reading of the same sections per municipality entry ( symbol_join_*.csv ), where the text layer supplies where every marker is and the model supplies which one it is — and the entry is refused whole if the two disagree on how many markers it has. Finding the headings is load-bearing for all of it, and the rule that found them was too narrow. It matched on the heading's first word, which is set in the largest face on the page and is therefore the worst-read text on it — Úřady arrives as Hřady , tířady , TJřady , Ĺ ř a d v . . That lost 137 of 1,146 headings , and a lost heading is not a lost section: its entries were being attached to the previous heading, so one district's institutions were filed under its neighbour's name. lexikon_1910_notes 0.4.0 anchors on the tail instead ( okresu X: ) and classifies the kind from fragments that survive the damage, which reproduces the old rule exactly on the 1,009 it found and recovers the rest. Channel B already establishes the floor these pages must beat, so the question a candidate reader answers is not "is it good" but "does it clear 87.7% on the same 308 blocks". Two things about a non-Claude reader change the arithmetic and are handled rather than assumed: No prompt caching. The system prompt is billed in full on every block instead of at a tenth on all but the first, so a per-token rate that looks cheaper is not automatically cheaper per block. --reader-price prices it honestly. Measures the pass rate and the cost *before* anything is committed to, on a source with no gold standard. The channels read the same pages without being told what the others said, and a deterministic grader that none of them can see scores the result: B the NDK ALTO text layer, snapped to the reconstructed grid (free) G the below-table apparatus, read from the image by an OCR model, returned as printed lines (billed, cheap) C the German volume, located by running head, both sides anchored to settlements_1910 and paired on the shared obec (free) A a vision model on a crop of a municipality block (billed, off by default) **The spend is deliberately unequal, because the source is.** Between the printed rules the ALTO reads digits at ~88%, and a second billed reading of a block that already satisfies every arithmetic identity buys confirmation of what was not in doubt. Below the rules it reads almost nothing worth having: the apparatus is small type, superscript keys, and — for most of what it records — *pictograms*, which no amount of parsing recovers from a text layer that never identified them. So the default run reads the apparatus with a model and the table without one. Channel A stays available for the blocks channel B failed (``--a-on-fail``), which is the only place a per-municipality rate is worth paying. The arithmetic is what makes that safe. The table has invariants; the apparatus has none, so its guard is a **closed vocabulary**: the reader may name a symbol only from the volume's own printed legend (*Výklad značek*, p. XI, carried in ``institution_abbreviations.csv``), and anything else is ``[?]``. A token off the list is rejected on arrival and counted in the ledger rather than normalised away. Channel G returns *printed lines*, not structure, so its output is assembled into the same ``Notes`` object the ALTO produces and every downstream consumer — section cutting, ``parts_check``, the postal legend, the institution decoder — runs on it unchanged. That is what makes the two readings comparable instead of merely both present. Every block is also anchored against the municipalities its okres is known to contain. That is the only check here that can see a block which should not exist, or a municipality the parser lost — no arithmetic identity can. The readers are the only model-specific part: everything downstream (grid, blocks, invariants, anchoring, grader) is indifferent to which model produced the rows, so a candidate reader can be scored on exactly the same yardstick. **The model never sees the invariants.** It is asked to transcribe what is printed and nothing else — no mention that the sexes sum to the total, that the confessions sum to the total, or that the settlements sum to their municipality. A model told what the numbers must add up to will return numbers that add up, and the pass rate stops measuring anything. For the same reason a failing block is re-read, never repaired: nothing that fails is quietly patched into the output. Two local models, two different jobs ------------------------------------ Run against a local Ollama daemon, the reading costs nothing and the constraint becomes wall-clock. It is worth splitting the work by what each model *is*: * **A dedicated OCR model** (``glm-ocr``: 0.9B, of which the language side is a 0.5B decoder) transcribes this print better than a general model its size, and cannot be asked to hold an 83-token taxonomy or a JSON schema while doing it. It gets ``--notes-style transcribe`` and ``--notes-format text``: every symbol comes back as ``[?]``, which still records the **position and the count** of each one, so the slots survive for a later pass. * **A general vision-language model** (``qwen3.5``, 4b/9b) can hold the closed list and the schema, so it gets ``--notes-style annotate`` and is the one that can actually *name* a post office or a school. Both defaults are inferred from the model id and announced. Run them as two labelled passes over the same pages and compare: the ``[?]`` slots from the first are exactly what the second has to fill, and both are graded against channel B by the same arithmetic. Why a section and not a column (``--notes-sections``) ---------------------------------------------------- The two passes above want different crops, and it took a failure to see it. A footnote column is ~1,350 x 1,000 px of six-point type; ``glm-ocr`` reads it in one call, and ``qwen3.5`` does not — on page 270 it returned the ``Části osad`` section and stopped, one line short of the ``Úřady`` heading and everything under it. Halving the column changed the failure mode rather than fixing it: the bottom halves came back well-formed and **empty**, which is worse, because a region with no lines reads downstream as a part of the page that was blank. So the crop is cut on the print instead. The register organises the apparatus into sections — one heading, one soudní okres, one kind — and the ALTO already knows where every heading sits, so ``--notes-sections offices`` sends each ``Úřady, ústavy`` section as its own image: a median of 478 px instead of a whole column, 1.77 crops a page instead of 3, a prompt that describes one kind of entry instead of five, and 56 symbol tokens instead of 83. What comes back is joined to the text layer's own reading of the same sections per municipality entry (``symbol_join_*.csv``), where the text layer supplies *where* every marker is and the model supplies *which* one it is — and the entry is refused whole if the two disagree on how many markers it has. Finding the headings is load-bearing for all of it, and the rule that found them was too narrow. It matched on the heading's first word, which is set in the largest face on the page and is therefore the worst-read text on it — ``Úřady`` arrives as ``Hřady``, ``tířady``, ``TJřady``, ``Ĺ ř a d v .``. That lost **137 of 1,146 headings**, and a lost heading is not a lost section: its entries were being attached to the previous heading, so one district's institutions were filed under its neighbour's name. ``lexikon_1910_notes`` 0.4.0 anchors on the tail instead (``okresu X:``) and classifies the kind from fragments that survive the damage, which reproduces the old rule exactly on the 1,009 it found and recovers the rest. This runner reads the German gold pages with the two readers the Czech r5 arms use, each three times: gemini38 Gemini 3.8 Flash, thinking off gemini38_r5atlasntgde{1,2,3} haiku55h Claude Haiku 5.5, thinking at high haiku55h_r5atlasgde{1,2,3} Everything a Czech r5 gold pass holds fixed is held fixed here — one section per call, both apparatus documents and the postal legend, strips cut through blank rows, upscaled, the volume's own symbol key sent with every crop, temperature 0 where the reader takes one — and three things are the German volume's own: the cut. The UBW scan has no text layer to cut on, so the pilot's channel G cannot run. The page is rendered at its native resolution, the geometry is lexikon_1910_image 's, and every heading is cut out and read by the pass's reader, then labelled by the German profile's matcher ( lexikon_1910_de_notes.cut_page ). A section open at the top of a page whose previous scan is not in the run takes its label from a read of that scan's last heading. Strips are 500 px × the page's scale (~375 px), the same amount of print as the Czech 500. what the reader is told. The Czech prompt with the German volume's words, and the German plate's 80 symbols — as the token list (the de rows of institution_abbreviations.csv ) and as the key image ( symbols/de/atlas_prompt.png ). the column header, read once a page and checked against the profile's seventeen labels (D-80, D-83: the German reader must report it). A German heading names a German court; its entries are filed under the Czech court's slug through the court crosswalk, so they share a key with the German gold sheets and with the Czech edition. Passes go to bakeoff/<host>/de/ — out of sight of every Czech table — and are scored by score_r5_german_notes.py . Certification sheets are never read. The frozen route (D-115) calls frozen_pass instead: any pages of any of the three German volumes, into a folder of its own, with the route's Haiku ( haiku55nh : the note for a reader that thinks, and the contrast sheet after the key), the reader of record saving its section crops ( section_images.py , scaled so the print is the size E3 learned it at) and, with a queue, every uncached crop written as a batch line ( reader_batches.py ) instead of being sent. of ``r5``: the German edition's apparatus, read by the r5 readers (D-92). D-58 makes the German *Spezialortsrepertorium von Böhmen* (Wien 1915) a second measurement of the register's institutions once its sections can be cut from the image, and D-67 gives it its own gold, matched to the Czech by court and municipality name. This runner reads the German gold pages with the two readers the Czech r5 arms use, each three times: gemini38 Gemini 3.8 Flash, thinking off gemini38_r5atlasntgde{1,2,3} haiku55h Claude Haiku 5.5, thinking at high haiku55h_r5atlasgde{1,2,3} Everything a Czech r5 gold pass holds fixed is held fixed here — one section per call, both apparatus documents and the postal legend, strips cut through blank rows, upscaled, the volume's own symbol key sent with every crop, temperature 0 where the reader takes one — and three things are the German volume's own: * **the cut.** The UBW scan has no text layer to cut on, so the pilot's channel G cannot run. The page is rendered at its native resolution, the geometry is ``lexikon_1910_image``'s, and *every* heading is cut out and read by the pass's reader, then labelled by the German profile's matcher (``lexikon_1910_de_notes.cut_page``). A section open at the top of a page whose previous scan is not in the run takes its label from a read of that scan's last heading. Strips are ``500 px × the page's scale`` (~375 px), the same amount of print as the Czech 500. * **what the reader is told.** The Czech prompt with the German volume's words, and the German plate's 80 symbols — as the token list (the ``de`` rows of ``institution_abbreviations.csv``) and as the key image (``symbols/de/atlas_prompt.png``). * **the column header,** read once a page and checked against the profile's seventeen labels (D-80, D-83: the German reader must report it). A German heading names a German court; its entries are filed under the Czech court's slug through the court crosswalk, so they share a key with the German gold sheets and with the Czech edition. Passes go to ``bakeoff/<host>/de/`` — out of sight of every Czech table — and are scored by ``score_r5_german_notes.py``. D-97 measured what that call would face on the twelve gold pages: ≈ 115 disputed claims a pair, with Gemini right in ≈ 59 % of them. So the free alternative to the call is always side with Gemini , and D-98 wrote the bar Opus has to clear against it before anything was sent. What is asked The pair is the reader of record against the second reader, gemini38_r5atlasntg1 × haiku55nh_r5atlasg1 , at settlement level on the entries both and the gold read ( claim_sets ). A part is sent when it holds a disputed claim — one of the two makes it, the other does not (the 106 claims the D-98 bar is measured on), or an agreed claim DINOv3 disagrees with on the reader of record's box (reported beside the bar; D-98 as amended). One call per part. Each outlined mark is one question, which token is printed here? , among its options ( options_for ): the tokens the readers placed on it, DINOv3's, the same base with other brackets or letters ( glyph_composites.csv ) and the confusion partners measured on the other gold pages, plus none of these and cannot tell . The marks asked are those of the disputed claims, of the flagged agreed ones, and — at no extra call — the agreed marks DINOv3 leaves unconfirmed in a part that is sent anyway. A disputed claim the locator put no box on keeps a presence question: printed / not printed / cannot tell . The call shows the symbol key the readers saw (cached with the instructions), the municipality's whole entry (1.3.0, entry_bands ) — every line of it, in both sections and across a section break — with the asked marks outlined and numbered, each mark enlarged, and for every token on offer a reference card: the plate's glyph and up to two cuts of it from other gold pages. It is never told which reader made which claim. claim_verdicts turns the answers back into presence per claim, so the D-98 measures are computed exactly as written. Effort low , Batch API (half price), prompt cache; three repeats, one batch each (each request carries the key as ≈ 0.9 MB of base64, and three repeats in one batch near the 256 MB cap). The part arm (1.2.0, D-101) --arm part asks one thing more of each outlined mark: whose mark is it? — an institution of the municipality as a whole ( 0 ), of a numbered part (its number), or the type mark of a part ( type:<name> : the one mark after a part's name that says what kind of place it is — a mill, a manor farm, a hamlet), which is no institution at all. A mark Opus files under another part moves there; a type mark leaves the inventory. The parts and their type marks come from the readers' own parts lists, as they would in the volume run.
