1409 1410 1411 1412 1413 1414 1415 1416 1417 1418 1419 1420 1421 1422 """Test B — does one Opus verify call settle what Gemini and Haiku dispute? (D-72, D-89, D-98) The route of D-72 reads every apparatus crop twice, with Gemini 3.8 Flash (the reader of record) and Claude Haiku 5.5, and sends a claim only one of them makes to a verify call; DINOv3 (E3) names every boxed glyph beside them. D-97 measured what that call would face on the twelve gold pages: ≈ 115 disputed claims a pair, with Gemini right in ≈ 59 % of them. So the free alternative to the call is **always side with Gemini**, and D-98 wrote the bar Opus has to clear against it before anything was sent. What is asked ------------- The pair is the reader of record against the second reader, ``gemini38_r5atlasntg1`` × ``haiku55nh_r5atlasg1``, at settlement level on the entries both and the gold read (:func:`claim_sets`). A part is sent when it holds * a **disputed** claim — one of the two makes it, the other does not (the 106 claims the D-98 bar is measured on), or * an **agreed** claim DINOv3 **disagrees** with on the reader of record's box (reported beside the bar; D-98 as amended). One call per part. Each **outlined mark** is one question, *which token is printed here?*, among its options (:func:`options_for`): the tokens the readers placed on it, DINOv3's, the same base with other brackets or letters (``glyph_composites.csv``) and the confusion partners measured on the **other** gold pages, plus ``none of these`` and ``cannot tell``. The marks asked are those of the disputed claims, of the flagged agreed ones, and — at no extra call — the agreed marks DINOv3 leaves unconfirmed in a part that is sent anyway. A disputed claim the locator put no box on keeps a presence question: ``printed`` / ``not printed`` / ``cannot tell``. The call shows the symbol key the readers saw (cached with the instructions), the municipality's **whole entry** (1.3.0, :func:`entry_bands`) — every line of it, in both sections and across a section break — with the asked marks outlined and numbered, each mark enlarged, and for every token on offer a reference card: the plate's glyph and up to two cuts of it from other gold pages. It is never told which reader made which claim. :func:`claim_verdicts` turns the answers back into presence per claim, so the D-98 measures are computed exactly as written. Effort ``low``, Batch API (half price), prompt cache; three repeats, one batch each (each request carries the key as ≈ 0.9 MB of base64, and three repeats in one batch near the 256 MB cap). The ``part`` arm (1.2.0, D-101) ------------------------------- ``--arm part`` asks one thing more of each outlined mark: **whose mark is it?** — an institution of the municipality as a whole (``0``), of a numbered part (its number), or the *type mark* of a part (``type:<name>``: the one mark after a part's name that says what kind of place it is — a mill, a manor farm, a hamlet), which is no institution at all. A mark Opus files under another part moves there; a type mark leaves the inventory. The parts and their type marks come from the readers' own parts lists, as they would in the volume run. Its answers, usage and report go to ``output/verify_test_b_part``, beside the base arm's, never over them. Everything it reports is fixed here, before any sealed page was scored (written 2026-10-25, with the Czech certification run on disk and nothing yet scored against it). The point of the sealed half is that nothing was tuned on it; a metric chosen after seeing how the route did on it would spend that seal as surely as tuning a prompt would. What it reports, and why each one Claim level P / R / F1 on the settlement key (page, district, municipality, part, token) — the unit the analysis consumes, and the unit the gold run is scored on. A 95 % interval by page-clustered bootstrap : the pages are resampled with replacement (10,000 draws, seed 1910 — the project's own), the percentile interval reported. Eight pages are eight clusters, so this interval, not the point estimate, is the result. An interval from treating ~500 claims as independent would be about half as wide and would be wrong. entry_exact — the share of entries whose claim set matches the gold's exactly, which is what a settlement-level regressor actually needs. Count accuracy — among claims the route got right, the share whose printed count matches (the gold run reports 875 of 879; this is the sealed equivalent). Per symbol: sensitivity and specificity. Sensitivity is recall for that token. Specificity is over the entries where the gold does not print it: 1 − false claims / entries without it . Reported with the gold's count beside it, because most tokens will have too few instances here to carry a rate (the estimate from the gold's own mix is that 33 of 46 Czech symbols have fewer than ten). Two populations, both reported as printed — every entry the sealed sheets print. This is the headline: it is the route as it will read the volume, misses included. shared entries — entries both the gold and the route reached, which is the rule run_frozen.score_claims uses on the gold. Reported so the two numbers are comparable; it is not the headline, because dropping an entry the route never reached would hide exactly the failure the sealed half exists to measure. The author's own rulings are reported apart On a sealed page the author's ruling and the gold transcription are one person reading one print, so a claim settled that way is not independent of the truth it is scored against. Every headline is given twice: with those claims and without them. On the Czech run that is 3 of ~503 claims, so it moves the headline by at most a few tenths of a point — but the number is stated rather than assumed. What it refuses An edition whose sealed sheets are not all status: complete (the German four are cut and blank as this is written) — there is nothing to score against, and a partial sheet would read as the route inventing claims. A second run over the same edition: the result file is written once. --force overwrites it and the record says so, so a re-score can never be passed off as the first. It never writes the gold's own reference files: the sealed sheets are read into memory here, never into output/lexikon_1910_pilot/inventory_human.csv , which run_frozen.gold_rows loads and the 0.999 rests on. German Böhmen twice, and the German half pooled (1.2.0, D-136) Written 2026-10-26, before any German sealed page was transcribed or scored. German Böhmen is read with the Czech anchor (D-129), which Mähren and Schlesien, having no Czech twin, cannot have. Its record therefore carries the route as run and, beside it, without the anchor ( final_inventory_no_anchor.csv , run_frozen.without_anchor ). The German half is then scored once more pooled — de-pooled : Böhmen's four sealed pages without the anchor, Mähren's two and Schlesien's two, one population of eight page clusters, the same metrics as above — because that is the route the two volumes without a twin get. Each volume's own figures are reported beside it; with two pages each, for Mähren and Schlesien they are a check that the route still works on their scans, not a rate. The German plate has no cooperative mark: where the Czech volume prints the mark and then the letters ( [cooperative]: R, 2 K ), the German prints the letters bare ( R, 2 K ). 562 563 564 565 566 567 568 569 570 571 572 573 574 575 576 577 578 579 """Score the sealed certification pages — once, against metrics written down first. This is the one-shot scorer D-55 and the 2026-10-24 audit (§D) ask for. **Everything it reports is fixed here, before any sealed page was scored** (written 2026-10-25, with the Czech certification run on disk and nothing yet scored against it). The point of the sealed half is that nothing was tuned on it; a metric chosen after seeing how the route did on it would spend that seal as surely as tuning a prompt would. What it reports, and why each one --------------------------------- 1. **Claim level P / R / F1** on the settlement key ``(page, district, municipality, part, token)`` — the unit the analysis consumes, and the unit the gold run is scored on. 2. **A 95 % interval by page-clustered bootstrap**: the pages are resampled with replacement (10,000 draws, seed 1910 — the project's own), the percentile interval reported. Eight pages are eight clusters, so this interval, not the point estimate, is the result. An interval from treating ~500 claims as independent would be about half as wide and would be wrong. 3. **``entry_exact``** — the share of entries whose claim set matches the gold's exactly, which is what a settlement-level regressor actually needs. 4. **Count accuracy** — among claims the route got right, the share whose printed count matches (the gold run reports 875 of 879; this is the sealed equivalent). 5. **Per symbol: sensitivity and specificity.** Sensitivity is recall for that token. Specificity is over the entries where the gold does *not* print it: ``1 − false claims / entries without it``. Reported with the gold's count beside it, because most tokens will have too few instances here to carry a rate (the estimate from the gold's own mix is that 33 of 46 Czech symbols have fewer than ten). Two populations, both reported ------------------------------ * **as printed** — every entry the sealed sheets print. This is the headline: it is the route as it will read the volume, misses included. * **shared entries** — entries both the gold and the route reached, which is the rule ``run_frozen.score_claims`` uses on the gold. Reported so the two numbers are comparable; it is *not* the headline, because dropping an entry the route never reached would hide exactly the failure the sealed half exists to measure. The author's own rulings are reported apart ------------------------------------------- On a sealed page the author's ruling and the gold transcription are one person reading one print, so a claim settled that way is not independent of the truth it is scored against. Every headline is given twice: with those claims and without them. On the Czech run that is 3 of ~503 claims, so it moves the headline by at most a few tenths of a point — but the number is stated rather than assumed. What it refuses --------------- * An edition whose sealed sheets are not all ``status: complete`` (the German four are cut and blank as this is written) — there is nothing to score against, and a partial sheet would read as the route inventing claims. * A second run over the same edition: the result file is written once. ``--force`` overwrites it and the record says so, so a re-score can never be passed off as the first. * It never writes the gold's own reference files: the sealed sheets are read into memory here, never into ``output/lexikon_1910_pilot/inventory_human.csv``, which ``run_frozen.gold_rows`` loads and the 0.999 rests on. German Böhmen twice, and the German half pooled (1.2.0, D-136) ------------------------------------------------------------- Written 2026-10-26, before any German sealed page was transcribed or scored. German Böhmen is read with the Czech anchor (D-129), which Mähren and Schlesien, having no Czech twin, cannot have. Its record therefore carries the route **as run** and, beside it, **without the anchor** (``final_inventory_no_anchor.csv``, ``run_frozen.without_anchor``). The German half is then scored once more **pooled** — ``de-pooled``: Böhmen's four sealed pages without the anchor, Mähren's two and Schlesien's two, one population of eight page clusters, the same metrics as above — because that is the route the two volumes without a twin get. Each volume's own figures are reported beside it; with two pages each, for Mähren and Schlesien they are a check that the route still works on their scans, not a rate. Channel B (the NDK ALTO text layer) and channel A (a vision model) read the same municipality-block crops , and every row each returned is in table_rows_<label>.csv ( run_lexikon_1910_pilot.py ). The gold is section 1 of the calibration and purposive sheets — 403 rows on 13 pages — read in-process by read_transcription_md.read_sheet . Certification sheets are never read here. Matching A gold row and a channel row are paired per page by a weighted alignment that keeps printed order: a pair scores the similarity of the normalised names, plus a bonus when the printed number agrees, and no pair under MIN_PAIR is made. A gold row with no partner is missed : the crop did not hold it, or the reader dropped it — the same for both channels when the crop is to blame. The mezi tím vojsko lines are left out on the channel side, because the gold sheets do not transcribe them. What is compared name : the words of the place name — runs of two or more letters, case-folded — so the bracketed place-type tokens, the footnote marks ( *) ), the dot leaders, the part numbers and a pictogram the text layer turned into a stray letter ( Pankratz o ) do not count against a reading. A misspelt word does. name_strict keeps everything but the brackets, marks and leaders, and is reported beside it. Number columns: the digits, with the printed nil . and an empty cell equal. post_key and station_note : the text with every space removed. script-utils-reference_tools-occupations: TL;DR The Czech→HISCO dictionary flags keys review where the coding is not settled, and the rival codes behind those flags are scattered across four places: a semicolon list in link_hisco (the German bridge, where one German gloss reaches several HISCO codes), a single column for OccCANINE, a single column for CZ-ISCO, and free prose in note . No file anywhere holds the one shape in which "code A or code B?" can actually be answered — (key, candidate code, that code's English job title, that code's HISCLASS) . Reference tools · v2.1.1 · 684 lines · 7 public functions · 5 constants · used by nothing else · utils/reference_tools/occupations/build_conflict_workbook.py candidates build_conflicts build_czisco_only build_decisions verify_xlsx load_curation main ROOT HERE CURATION OUT_XLSX OUT_CSV How it works This builds it. One row per (key × candidate HISCO code) , every candidate carrying its own label and class, plus a moves column saying whether choosing it would change the social class at all — because most of these disputes do not. zámečník is HISCLASS 7 under all four of its candidates; the argument is real but it moves nothing downstream. CZ-ISCO is never a candidate. It is ISCO-08, ILO's crosswalks reach only ISCO-88, and HISCO is ISCO-68 — there is no path from a CZ-ISCO code to a HISCO code, which is why run_czisco_check.py asserts it never touches hisco . It travels here as evidence about the Czech reading, in its own columns and its own sheet, never as an option to pick. The workbook asks one question per word, not one per candidate. The long table above is the evidence; it is not the shape a decision is made in. A human answering "which code for kovář " needs one row, and only where the answer moves something. On the first build — 172 flagged keys, ~25.3k records — 76 had a rival that changed the HISCLASS and those were the sheet that opened; the 44 arguments that left the class where it was sat on a second sheet and the 52 keys with no rival at all on a third. Nine columns instead of twenty-five — the four candidate columns collapse into one wrapped cell (59 of the 76 were a plain A-or-B), the German gloss, the note and CZ-ISCO's verdict merge into one, and hisclass_basis , whose four values needed a paragraph of instructions to serve eleven rows, becomes a parenthesis in the cell it qualifies. The CSV twin keeps the full per-candidate shape. It builds from the live flag, so it shrinks as questions get answered. The 2026-08-26 pass settled 171 of 181 ( czech_glosses.ADJUDICATED ); the ten that survived are what the next build holds. A key already carrying a verdict is not asked about again — including on the CZ-ISCO sheet, which is not driven by review and would otherwise repeat itself every run. Nothing is written back. An accepted decision is applied by hand to czech_glosses.HISCO_OVERRIDE and the curation is rebuilt — same protocol as czisco_tail_candidates.csv . TL;DR CZ-ISCO (ČSÚ classification 80146, 2025) as a Czech→English occupational bridge , which is the one thing this project's occupation coding has never had. Reference tools · v1.0.0 · 232 lines · 5 public functions · 5 constants · used by utils/reference_tools/occupations/run_czisco_check.py · utils/reference_tools/occupations/build_czisco_bridge.py head_nouns matches_head build bridge_report main ROOT RAW OUT CS EN How it works Why it matters: every HISCO code here is reached through a German gloss ( obuvník → Schuhmacher ) that this project wrote. Both existing external checks inherit that weakness — the History of Work link bridge starts from our gloss, and OccCANINE had to be fed our gloss because Czech is not among its 13 training languages. Neither validates the claim "this Czech word means that occupation". CZ-ISCO does, because the Czech statistical office publishes the Czech and the English label under the same code. Two structural facts decide how it can be used, both asserted below: KLAS80146_CS.csv and KLAS80146_EN.csv join 1:1 on chodnota — 1,991 codes over five levels. English labels exist only at levels 1–4 (617 codes). All 1,374 five-digit national codes — the ones carrying actual trade names like Zámečníci strojů — have an empty text . They inherit English from their 4-digit ISCO-08 parent through nadvaz , which resolves for every one of them. So the bridge is Czech trade name → official English at ISCO-08 granularity , not at the Czech national level. What this is not : a source of HISCO codes. CZ-ISCO is the 2025 classification and the historical core of this corpus is simply absent from it — rolník , hajný , příručí , tkadlec , mlynář , kolář , bednář , cihlář , havíř and soustružník have no label at any level. Nor is there a path to HISCO: ISCO.pdf is ILO's ISCO-08 Volume I, whose correspondence tables reach ISCO- 88 , while HISCO is built on ISCO- 68 . Chaining two lossy crosswalks across forty years of occupational change, into a scheme designed for 1690–1970 data, would manufacture precision the sources do not carry. CZ-ISCO corroborates a reading; it never assigns a code. Run: python utils/reference_tools/occupations/build_czisco_bridge.py Emits: reference/occupations/czisco_authority.csv Consumed by utils/reference_tools/occupations/run_czisco_check.py (a validation script, not a pipeline input — the same standing as utils/reference_tools/units/build_unit_authority.py). Functions def head_nouns ( label : str ) -> list [ tuple [ str , bool ]] (head noun, is phrase-initial) for every coordinate phrase in a CZ-ISCO label. Stavební zámečníci -> zámečníci (leading adjective stripped) Zámečníci strojů -> zámečníci (genitive complement follows the head) Obchodní náměstci -> náměstci (so obchodník does not match) Řídící pracovníci ve studentských ubytovnách -> pracovníci (so student does not match — the failure this rule exists to prevent) Kováři, nástrojaři a příbuzní pracovníci -> three heads A phrase of adjectives only ( Kočí is indeclinable and looks like one) falls back to its first token, so a single-word label is always its own head. Both existing external checks inherit that weakness — the History of Work link bridge *starts* from our gloss, and OccCANINE had to be *fed* our gloss because Czech is not among its 13 training languages. Neither validates the claim "this Czech word means that occupation". CZ-ISCO does, because the Czech statistical office publishes the Czech and the English label under the same code. Two structural facts decide how it can be used, both asserted below: * ``KLAS80146_CS.csv`` and ``KLAS80146_EN.csv`` join 1:1 on ``chodnota`` — 1,991 codes over five levels. * **English labels exist only at levels 1–4** (617 codes). They inherit English from their 4-digit ISCO-08 parent through ``nadvaz``, which resolves for every one of them. So the bridge is *Czech trade name → official English at ISCO-08 granularity*, not at the Czech national level. What this is **not**: a source of HISCO codes. CZ-ISCO is the 2025 classification and the historical core of this corpus is simply absent from it — ``rolník``, ``hajný``, ``příručí``, ``tkadlec``, ``mlynář``, ``kolář``, ``bednář``, ``cihlář``, ``havíř`` and ``soustružník`` have no label at any level. Nor is there a path to HISCO: ``ISCO.pdf`` is ILO's ISCO-08 Volume I, whose correspondence tables reach ISCO-**88**, while HISCO is built on ISCO-**68**. Chaining two lossy crosswalks across forty years of occupational change, into a scheme designed for 1690–1970 data, would manufacture precision the sources do not carry. CZ-ISCO corroborates a reading; it never assigns a code. Encyklopedie československých legií. Praha: Universum. Why this exists unit_authority.csv says that a unit existed, in which theatre and from when. It does not say where the unit stood in a given month, and that is what a design with time-varying exposure needs: the shocks of the Russian theatre (November 1917, Brest- Litovsk, May 1918, the withdrawal from the front in 1919) hit every unit at once, so the only variation with a comparison group is which unit was at the front, in a garrison or on the rails when . The encyclopedia writes exactly that, in one formula per entry, down to the battalion: Nacházelo se v -> Borispolu, od prosince 1917 na přesunu a v -> Kajevce, od března 1918 ..., podléhalo veliteli -> X, od října 1917 veliteli -> Y. Funkci velitele pluku zastávali plk. A (srpen 1917 – září 1917), ... Each formula becomes rows of one long table: kind = location state ∈ {place, moving, field, moving_home}; value = the place, in the grammatical case the source uses ("Borispolu") kind = parent value = the formation the unit answered to; state says which of two chains it is when the source gives two (professional, general) kind = commander value = rank and name, with the months of the tenure; state = the office when it is not the commander's (chief_of_staff, …) kind = lifecycle state ∈ {formed, renamed, merged, disbanded, sailed, arrived_home}; value = the unit it came from or became kind = composition (transports) the units that sailed kind = strength (transports) how many men Dates are as precise as the source: a lifecycle date is a day, a phase of the location and subordination chains opens in a month ("od prosince 1917"), and the first phase of a chain opens when the unit was formed ( date_from_precision = formation ). Several states inside one phase share its opening month and keep the order the source gives them in seq ; the source does not date the changes inside a phase. What it does NOT carry: detachments the source puts in brackets ("části oddílu v X"), and anything the entry says outside its formulas. The source's slips are kept and flagged, not corrected. A location chain that runs backwards in time ("od prosince 1919 v Čeljabinsku, od ledna 1919 na přesunu" — the year of one of the two is a misprint) keeps the dates as printed; the rows outside the longest run that is in order carry date_suspect = 1 . A sub-entry heading printed twice under one headword gets "#2" on its second occurrence. Copyright note As for build_unit_authority.py : the book is in copyright and stays in the gitignored library/ . This script emits facts only (unit, date, place, formation, name) and none of the encyclopedia's prose. Why this exists --------------- ``unit_authority.csv`` says that a unit existed, in which theatre and from when. It does not say where the unit stood in a given month, and that is what a design with time-varying exposure needs: the shocks of the Russian theatre (November 1917, Brest- Litovsk, May 1918, the withdrawal from the front in 1919) hit every unit at once, so the only variation with a comparison group is *which unit was at the front, in a garrison or on the rails when*. The encyclopedia writes exactly that, in one formula per entry, down to the battalion: Nacházelo se v -> Borispolu, od prosince 1917 na přesunu a v -> Kajevce, od března 1918 ..., podléhalo veliteli -> X, od října 1917 veliteli -> Y. Funkci velitele pluku zastávali plk. A (srpen 1917 – září 1917), ... Each formula becomes rows of one long table: kind = location state ∈ {place, moving, field, moving_home}; value = the place, in the grammatical case the source uses ("Borispolu") kind = parent value = the formation the unit answered to; state says which of two chains it is when the source gives two (professional, general) kind = commander value = rank and name, with the months of the tenure; state = the office when it is not the commander's (chief_of_staff, …) kind = lifecycle state ∈ {formed, renamed, merged, disbanded, sailed, arrived_home}; value = the unit it came from or became kind = composition (transports) the units that sailed kind = strength (transports) how many men Dates are as precise as the source: a lifecycle date is a day, a phase of the location and subordination chains opens in a month ("od prosince 1917"), and the first phase of a chain opens when the unit was formed (``date_from_precision = formation``). Several states inside one phase share its opening month and keep the order the source gives them in ``seq``; the source does not date the changes inside a phase. What it does NOT carry: detachments the source puts in brackets ("části oddílu v X"), and anything the entry says outside its formulas. The source's slips are kept and flagged, not corrected. A location chain that runs backwards in time ("od prosince 1919 v Čeljabinsku, od ledna 1919 na přesunu" — the year of one of the two is a misprint) keeps the dates as printed; the rows outside the longest run that is in order carry ``date_suspect = 1``. A sub-entry heading printed twice under one headword gets "#2" on its second occurrence. Reference tools · v1.0.0 · 217 lines · 3 public functions · 9 constants · used by nothing else · utils/reference_tools/education/check_unterricht_transcription.py Result check_table main ROOT HERE ROLLUPS ROLLUPS_T34 TABLES ROW_SUMS SUBSETS N_LANDS KNOWN_SOURCE_ERRATA How it works Three tables of the volume are transcribed by hand from an image-only scan into unterricht_t{19,20,34}_*.csv . Reading a printed table off a photographed page is the one step in this project with a known failure mode: check_atlas_parties.py exists because a row-offset in a table read off a curved page produced a plausible set of numbers that only a cross-reference caught. The same risk applies here and is larger, because these are numeric columns where a slipped row leaves no grammatical trace at all. What makes the check possible is that the volume over-determines itself. Every table prints both the parts and their roll-up: Küstenland is Triest + Görz und Gradisca + Istrien, Tirol und Vorarlberg is its two halves, the last row is the column total, and in Table 34 the eight class-count columns must sum across to the school total on the same row. None of that is used to build the CSVs — it is arithmetic the printer already did, so agreement is evidence the read is right rather than evidence the file is self-consistent. Every failure is reported with the row and column, because the point is to find the slipped line, not to learn that one exists. Run: python utils/reference_tools/education/check_unterricht_transcription.py Emits: nothing — prints PASS/FAIL per invariant. German is the right bridge for this corpus — these are 1910 Bohemian, Moravian and Silesian occupational titles, whose German equivalents the HISCO project has already coded ( hisco_occupation_link_combined.csv , 1,199 distinct German labels) — and it is also one of OccCANINE's 13 training languages, so the same gloss feeds the independent check. The English gloss is the fallback lookup against the authority's own label_en . Only atomic keys are glossed. Compounds are decomposed by utils.parsing.occupations.split_occupations on token boundaries, so rolník zedník , mlynářský dělník and waiter číšník need no entry of their own. HISCO_OVERRIDE carries codes decided by hand — where the bridge is ambiguous, where the German equivalent does not exist, or where a documented judgement call is needed (see reference/OCCUPATION_CODING.md ). ADJUDICATED is the answer sheet: every key the 2026-08-26 conflict workbook put in front of a human, and what came back. It is the only thing that clears a review flag, so a word that is still flagged is one nobody has settled — not one nobody has read. """ czech_glosses.py — Czech occupational key -> German / English gloss =================================================================== The authored half of the occupation pipeline, and the piece no external source supplies: neither the History of Work title dictionary nor OccCANINE covers Czech. Rather than assign HISCO codes from memory, each Czech key gets a **German** gloss. German is the right bridge for this corpus — these are 1910 Bohemian, Moravian and Silesian occupational titles, whose German equivalents the HISCO project has already coded (``hisco_occupation_link_combined.csv``, 1,199 distinct German labels) — and it is also one of OccCANINE's 13 training languages, so the same gloss feeds the independent check. The English gloss is the fallback lookup against the authority's own ``label_en``. Only **atomic** keys are glossed. Compounds are decomposed by ``utils.parsing.occupations.split_occupations`` on token boundaries, so ``rolník zedník``, ``mlynářský dělník`` and ``waiter číšník`` need no entry of their own. ``HISCO_OVERRIDE`` carries codes decided by hand — where the bridge is ambiguous, where the German equivalent does not exist, or where a documented judgement call is needed (see ``reference/OCCUPATION_CODING.md``). ``ADJUDICATED`` is the answer sheet: every key the 2026-08-26 conflict workbook put in front of a human, and what came back. It is the only thing that clears a ``review`` flag, so a word that is still flagged is one nobody has settled — not one nobody has read. Okres-level composition cannot clear any individual record, and it separates own-account from wage-earning but not the holder from the farmer's son. This check goes at exactly that limit. The Vienna Database on European Family History (unharmonized Austrian numeric file, distributed by MOSAIC) records 163,400 individuals in 44 localities, 1632–1947, from census data and libri status animarum . Every person carries an occupation drawn from a closed list of 521 German nominal titles and , independently, a household position — Haushaltsvorstand, Hausfrau, Sohn, Gesindeperson. That pairing is what no other source in this project has: it shows, person by person, what the German occupational vocabulary the project's own glosses are written in actually denoted. The coding was done 1974–1984 at the University of Vienna, so it is independent of this project in the strong sense: it predates it. Cite as: Vienna Database on European Family History . Numeric data file, Version 0.1 [SPSS file]. Vienna: University of Vienna, 2003. ( reference/DATA_SOURCES.md #14.) Three things follow, and the script tests them in that order: The vocabulary is split at source . BAUER and LANDARBEITER/KNECHT are different entries on the same closed list, in different berufs systematic classes. A recording tradition that kept a separate word for the hired hand was not using BAUER to mean one. The split shows up in household position — the individual-level fact Check 6 lacks. Restricted to males 18–30 , the Legion age band, it also answers the farmer's-son half: a farmer's son appears on these listings as SOHN, not as BAUER. What this cannot do, and the write-up must keep saying so. It validates the German term , not the Czech reading — the same gap Checks 1 and 2 carry. rolník 's gloss in czech_glosses.py is Landwirt ; the term present here is Bauer (this project's gloss for sedlák ), and a bare LANDWIRT is not on the 521-term list at all, so the bridge runs through a Landwirt ≈ Bauer synonymy this check assumes rather than demonstrates. It is also the wrong territory (44 Austrian localities, no Czech lands) and largely the wrong period (bulk 1857). Most important: household position and occupational title are not independent in a Seelenbeschreibung — one clerk assigned both — so this corroborates Check 6, it does not independently prove it. dělník → 99900 is deliberately out of scope. The Arbeiter family (HANDARBEITER, FABRIKARBEITER, HILFSARBEITER) is present in the source, but that is a different question and this check does not open it. Reference tools · v1.0.0 · 401 lines · 6 public functions · 7 constants · used by nothing else · utils/reference_tools/education/run_unterricht_check.py run_taxonomy run_continuation run_klassen run_composition run_language main ROOT HERE FIN CZECH_LANDS PLACEBO_LANDS LAND_COL CZECH_LANDS_SAMPLE How it works The scheme in utils/parsing/education.py was built from two secondary works — Moore (2020) for the general ladder, Lassnigg (2015) for the vocational branch. Neither is a count of schools: Moore describes the law, and Lassnigg's own quantitative series begins in 1924 , in the Republic of Austria, on territory this sample does not cover. So the six rungs, and in particular the decision to keep the pokračovací continuation school off the ordinal, have never been checked against a source that could contradict them. Nothing else in the project can do it. data_checks.py asks whether the columns are mutually consistent, which they would be if the whole scheme were wrong; the Fidler check reaches units, not schools; and the occupation checks use education as a predictor without ever validating it. VALIDATION.md lists education only under "What none of them reach". The source here is the administration's own annual census of its schools — Österreichische Statistik XCIII/1, Statistik der Unterrichtsanstalten … für das Jahr 1908/1909 (Wien 1912) — transcribed to unterricht_t{19,20,34}_*.csv and gated by check_unterricht_transcription.py . It is contemporaneous with the years this cohort was at school, it covers Böhmen, Mähren and Schlesien specifically, and it splits every school type by Unterrichtssprache , so the benchmark can be restricted to Czech-language institutions rather than to all of Cisleithania. What this cannot do Hungary. The volume is "in den im Reichsrate vertretenen Königreichen und Ländern" — Cisleithania by definition. Slovak and Rusyn births are outside it, and D-08 stays open on exactly that. Every test below restricts to Cisleithanian-born records and says so. Flow versus stock. The volume counts pupils enrolled in one year, 1908/09. The legionnaire field records the schooling of men born mostly 1875-1900, i.e. an accumulated stock observed years later. The two are not the same quantity and a share from one is not an estimate of the other. run_composition therefore tests ordering and magnitude , with a placebo, and never equality — a close match would be luck, not corroboration. Institutions versus pupils. Tables 20 and 34 count schools; some columns count pupils. A ratio of school counts is not a ratio of people, and where only school counts exist the test says so rather than pretending otherwise. Nothing here is causal, and nothing here writes. Run: python utils/reference_tools/education/run_unterricht_check.py Emits: nothing — prints the result for reference/VALIDATION_EDUCATION.md . This is a validation script, never a pipeline input; it writes no file and touches no code column. re . compile ( '(?Somewhere on a Czech government server there are 133,000 web pages, one per legionnaire, each a little table of half-filled fields typed up from a paper card: born Kolín, trade zámečník, joined 12.3.1917. A person can read one of those in a few seconds. Nobody can read 133,000, and no statistical model can read even one — a model wants a rectangle of numbers, and this is a heap of Czech sentences.
The pipeline is the machine that turns the heap into the rectangle, and it is built in three stages so that each can be checked. Collect: fetch the pages and store them exactly as they came, never touched again. Clean: read every field with a small specialist — one for dates, one for ranks, one for jobs, one for places — and write out a table where a column means the same thing in every row. Visualise: draw the pictures, and read only from that final table, so a figure can never quietly disagree with the data it claims to show.
The rule that makes the whole thing survivable is that the raw copy is sacred. Every judgement — every guess, every repair, every dropped record — happens in the middle stage, in code, where it can be read, argued with and undone. If a decision made in 2026 turns out to be wrong, the fix is one function and a re-run, not a dataset nobody can reconstruct.

Imagine posting a letter addressed only to Nová Ves, Bohemia. There are dozens of Nová Ves — New Village is the Czech Springfield — and the one you want stopped existing under that name in 1918, was called something else in German, and has since been swallowed by a town. That is the problem on every one of these birth records, and it has to be solved 300,000 times, because a soldier's birthplace is how he gets attached to the 1910 census: how literate his district was, how many Czechs and Germans lived in it, how much of it farmed.
So the matcher works like a careful postal clerk rather than a clever one. It tries the strongest evidence first — does this string name a district outright? — then weaker and weaker readings: a court district, a village in the gazetteer, a near-miss spelling. Crucially it writes down which rung it used. Every record carries a label saying how confident the match is, so an analysis can throw the weak ones away and see whether the result survives.
Two things it refuses to do. It will not break a tie by picking whichever candidate the lookup table happened to list first — a coin-flip dressed as an answer. And it will not place a village in Slovakia just because a Slovak village has the same name, when the record says the man was born in Galicia. Where the evidence genuinely runs out, the field stays empty, and empty is a finding.

In 1916 the imperial statistical office printed a book that lists every inhabited place in Bohemia — every village, every hamlet, every mill with a name. For each one it gives a row of numbers: how many hectares, how many houses, how many people, how many Catholics, how many spoke Czech. That part is a spreadsheet that happens to be made of paper, and a computer reads it about as well as you would expect: nine numbers in ten come out right.
The interesting part is underneath. In tiny type at the foot of every page, the book also records what each village had — a school, a midwife, a fire brigade, a savings bank, a post office, a Czech credit union rather than a German one. That is a completely different kind of fact from a headcount, and nothing else in this project comes close to it: you can measure whether a man grew up somewhere with institutions or somewhere with none. There is one problem. To save space, the 1916 typesetter printed those institutions not as words but as little pictures — a tiny open book for a school, a stylised helmet for a fire brigade — and defined them once, on a key page at the front.
A computer cannot read a picture it has never been shown. Text-recognition software sees the school symbol and confidently types g. Modern AI models, asked what the mark is, guess — and guess differently from each other: handed the identical symbol, two of them answered “doctor” and “curate”. Over one test page they agreed with each other about the words of an entry two times in three, and about the symbols about one time in ten.
So the work splits in two. The numbers upstairs are read by machine and then made to prove themselves: men plus women must equal the total, the villages must add up to their parish. Crucially the machine is never told what the answer should be — tell it the total and it will happily produce numbers that reach that total, and the test stops testing anything. Downstairs there is no such arithmetic, nothing adds up to anything, and the only defences are a fixed list of names a reader is allowed to use, and a human sitting down with the key page. A person reading those marks by hand got 286 of them and was unsure about none, which settles one thing at least: the difficulty is not the scan. It is that we are asking machines to recognise a picture nobody has drawn for them.

Every soldier's card has one word for what he did: rolník, zámečník, obchodní příručí. To ask whether poor men deserted more often than comfortable ones, those words have to become something comparable — a rung on a ladder that a farmer in Moravia and a clerk in Prague can both stand on.
That is what HISCO is: an international coding scheme where every historical job has a five-digit number, and every number maps to a social class from 1 (elite) to 13 (unskilled). The trouble is that HISCO was built from Dutch, English and German records and contains no Czech at all. So the dictionary from Czech word to code is written here, by hand, one entry at a time — about 500 entries, which is enough to cover 98.5  % o f the men because occupations follow a brutal power law: a handful of trades account for most of a population.
The matching itself is deliberately stupid. It will accept a phrase only if a whole run of words is already in the dictionary — never a fragment inside a word. That stupidity is the safety feature: a cleverer matcher, allowed to look inside words, once found the rank major hiding inside generálmajor and demoted every general in the army. Here, if nothing matches, the answer is nothing.
And the honest part: about a fifth of the coded records rest on a judgement that could have gone the other way. Rolník — a sixth of the whole sample — is read as a farmer who works his own land rather than a hired farmhand, which is a four-class difference. That single call was tested against the 1910 census's own employment columns before it was allowed to stand, and it is flagged in the data so anyone can re-run the analysis without it.
" , 'ranks' : "
The central question of this project is what a demotion does to a man. A legionnaire had already deserted the Austrian army once; some of them were sergeants or lieutenants when they did. In the Czechoslovak Legion many started again as privates. Did the ones who fell furthest desert again?
To ask that, the two armies' rank systems have to be laid side by side, and they do not line up on their own — different languages, different numbers of grades, and titles that mean different things in each. So both are placed on one ordinal scale using the NATO officer codes as the bridge, and the drop is simply the difference: a Habsburg sergeant who becomes a Legion private has a rank reset of minus several rungs.
The trap here is a title that is not a grade at all. Some men were entered as pracovník (labour service) or občan (civilian) — administrative holding categories on the way in, not punishments. Scored naively, a Habsburg colonel entering as a labourer looks like the most spectacular demotion in the dataset, and it never happened. Those 7,696 records are flagged, and the headline result is computed without them.
" , 'ranks-legal' : '
When the war ended, hundreds of thousands of men who had worn one uniform had to be fitted into another — and the new Czechoslovak state had to decide what their old rank was worth. This sheet is the answer, dug out of the statute books.
The law was openly lopsided, and knowing that is the point. Legion service was a reward: preferential appointments, generous crediting of time served, seniority back-dated as far as 1914. Former Austro-Hungarian officers were let in grudgingly and often a grade down. Two men of identical ability ended the decade in different places purely because of which army they had been in.
It sits in the documentation because it explains a rumour the data would otherwise seem to support. Legionnaires believed officers were being demoted; the statutes show the opposite policy. So when the data shows a Habsburg officer entering the Legion at a low grade, the explanation is an entry procedure, not a punishment — and that distinction changes what the desertion result means.
' , 'units' : "
A soldier's record says he served in the 1st Regiment. Which one? The Czechoslovak Legion in Russia had a 1st Regiment. So did the Legion in Italy. So did the French Foreign Legion, in which a Czech company also fought. Three different wars, three different sets of men, one number.
Treating them as one unit would be a real error, not a cosmetic one, because unit is how soldiers are grouped for almost every comparison in the project — how big was his company, how many of his comrades died, did his regiment desert as a bloc. Mix two regiments together and every one of those numbers is wrong.
The fix is to stop using the number alone and use regiment plus army as the identity. It sounds trivial; it moved 4,347 records, and it revealed that the records labelled 1st Regiment are mostly Foreign Legion rather than the Czechoslovak 1st Rifles that everyone assumes.
" , 'habsburg-army' : "
The Habsburg army recruited locally on purpose. Each regiment had a home district it drew its men from, so a regiment was in effect a slice of one region — its language, its trades, its villages. That is the Ergänzung system, and it is why a regiment number is quietly also a place.
That link is worth a great deal here. It lets a man's pre-Legion unit be tied back to a census district even when his own birthplace field is unreadable, and it gives a way to ask whether men from the same home district behaved alike — the kind of comparison the whole literature on unit cohesion turns on.
It also explains the ambiguity next door: the Monarchy ran three parallel armies — the common army, the Austrian Landwehr and the Hungarian Honvéd — each numbering its own regiments from one, each with its own command language. A bare number is genuinely ambiguous, which is not sloppiness in the records but a fact about the state that kept them.
" , 'provenance' : '
A finished number in a paper — desertion in Russia was four percent — hides a chain of sources behind it: a scraped website, a census workbook, a shapefile, a hand-written dictionary. If any link is weak, the number is weak, and by the time it reaches a table nobody can tell which link it was.
This sheet keeps the chain visible. Every mechanism the project claims is drawn back to the source that grounds it, so the reader can see at a glance which claims rest on an official census, which on a scholarly encyclopedia, and which on a judgement made here.
It is also a defence against a specific kind of self-deception: a source used for two different purposes starts to look like two independent confirmations. Drawn as a graph, that shows up immediately as one node with two arrows out of it — which is one piece of evidence, not two.
' , 'architecture' : '
This project is about forty Python modules that call each other. That is small enough to feel manageable and quite large enough to hide a nasty surprise: you change how one function reads a date, and something four steps downstream that you had forgotten depends on it starts producing plausible, wrong answers.
So the import graph is drawn automatically from the source itself — never from a hand-kept list, which would be out of date within a week. Click a module and the map highlights everything that would feel a change to it.
The practical use is before an edit, not after. If the blast radius of a one-line change is eleven modules, that is worth knowing while the change is still an idea.
' , 'validation-register' : '
Most projects report the checks that passed. This one has a column for what each check cannot see, and that column is the honest half.
The distinction that organises it: an external check compares this project against a source that could genuinely contradict it — a published encyclopedia, an official census, an independently trained model. A self-check only confirms that the output obeys the rules it was built from. Self-checks are necessary and they are not evidence that the coding is right; a rule applied perfectly to the wrong data passes every one of them.
Reading the blind-spot column is the fastest way to find out what this project does not know. Place matching below the district level, for instance, has no external check at all — so it is written down as unchecked rather than left to look like it passed.
' , 'validation' : "
The best thing that can happen to a dataset is that somebody who has never seen it wrote down the answers first. In 2025 a historian published an encyclopedia of the Czechoslovak Legions: which units existed, where they fought, when they formed. That is an answer key produced with no knowledge of this project whatsoever.
Checked against it, the pipeline's theatre assignment agrees on 99.6  % o f records, and every officer rank resolves correctly. More usefully, it found two real bugs. The rank ladder had no general grades, so generálmajor matched the word major and every Legion general was recorded three rungs too low. And notes about a rank — candidate for lieutenant, was not a soldier — were being scored as that rank.
It also found roughly 130 records where the source website contradicts the historical record: regiments placed in Russia that only ever existed in France. Those are documented and left alone. Silently correcting a source is how a dataset stops being evidence about the source.
" , 'validation-education' : "
What a soldier wrote in the schooling box — ob. 5 mě. 3 and the like — only means something if you know what those schools were. Until now that knowledge came from two modern history books. Neither counts schools; one of them starts its figures in 1924, in a different country.
This page checks the scheme against the thing itself: the Austrian government's own annual census of every school it ran, printed in Vienna in 1912 for the year 1908/09, with a table for each kind of school in each province and the language it taught in. It is the register the ladder should have been built on, and it says three things.
It confirms the awkward call at the heart of the variable. The pokračovací school — compulsory evening classes for apprentices — had been treated as a rung above the rest, which would have made an apprentice look better-educated than a grammar-school boy. The government filed it in a category of its own, and it was enormous: 504 of them in Bohemia teaching 50,836 pupils, against nine state trade schools teaching 3,518. Leaving it off the ladder was right.
It breaks something else. The code marks an elementary schooling “complete” at eight years, because the law required eight years of schooling. But the census counts schools by how many year-groups they actually had, and a eight-class elementary school existed ten times in the whole empire and twice in the Czech lands. Nearly four thousand men are recorded as having finished a school that was almost nowhere, and three thousand more who wrote down the ordinary full five years are marked as having dropped out. The column is being left alone until that is decided properly rather than patched.
And it shows that the evening classes are badly under-recorded: in life there were five of those pupils for every full-time trade-school pupil, but in these records there are fewer than one. Men simply did not write down the classes they were obliged to attend. So that flag counts some apprentices, not all of them.
What none of it touches is Hungary. The volume covers only the Austrian half of the monarchy, and about ten thousand men here were schooled in the Hungarian half under different laws. That gap is old, and it stays.
" , 'validation-occupations' : "
The Czech-to-HISCO dictionary is the part of this project with the most human judgement in it, so it gets three independent second opinions, each blind to the others — and then two more aimed at the single word that carries a sixth of the sample.
The German bridge translates each Czech job into its 1910 German equivalent and looks that up in the international database — useful precisely because Habsburg records were kept in German, so the translation is contemporary rather than modern. OccCANINE is a neural network trained on millions of historical job titles in other languages; fed the same German glosses, it agrees on 88  % o f records at the class level. CZ-ISCO is the modern Czech statistical classification — the only source that tests the Czech reading itself rather than a translation of it.
Each is blind in a different place, which is the point of having three. The German bridge cannot catch a mistranslation. OccCANINE cannot tell a clerk from an attendant, because that distinction is administrative and not in the title. CZ-ISCO is 2025 usage, so where a trade has drifted in a century it disagrees for the right reason and the wrong period — and it reaches none of the old rural words the sample is actually full of.
Which leaves the word none of them can reach. Rolník is a sixth of the sample and the difference between reading it as a farmer who owns his land and a hired farmhand is four social classes. So it gets its own two checks. The 1910 census carries columns for whether a man farmed on his own account or for wages, district by district: where the census counts more own-account farmers, the legionnaires from that district are more owner-coded — which is an argument about districts and never about one man. The Vienna Database supplies the missing half, because it records people one at a time: among men aged 18–30, a Bauer is 97.5  % a household head and 0.3  % a son. A farmer's son is not what the word names. Wrong territory, and the title and the position were written down by the same clerk — so it narrows the doubt rather than closing it.
" , 'decisions' : "
Building a dataset means making hundreds of choices that could defensibly have gone the other way, and the danger is not making them badly — it is making them invisibly. Six months later nobody, including the author, can tell which numbers are measurements and which are consequences of a forgotten decision.
So every such choice gets a line here: what was decided, why, and whether it is settled, provisional (in force, but the alternative would change results) or open. The argument itself is not repeated — it stays in whichever document already makes it, and this is the index.
The provisional ones are the interesting ones. They are the places where the paper's results depend on a call that a reasonable person could reject, stated in advance rather than discovered by a referee.
" , 'audit' : '
Twice — once in July 2026 and again in September — the entire codebase was read line by line, deliberately looking for reasons to distrust it rather than reasons to ship it. This sheet is what the two passes found, newest first.
The September pass found its worst problem in the step that matches a legionnaire to the same man in the list of fallen Habsburg soldiers. Two records were called the same person when the names were similar enough — but the test scored the whole name at once, so a shared first name (there are a great many Františeks) could carry two different surnames over the line. A second rule trusted a note field that mostly says which regiment keeps the death register, not that the man served in the Legion. Once each part of the name had to match on its own and the note had to actually mention the Legion, the 2,239 matched men fell to 1,340. Fewer matches, but ones that are really the same person.
The July pass found the one below, and it is worth understanding even if you never touch the code.
It is the most dangerous shape a data bug takes. About 26,000 soldiers had a blank exit field — nothing was recorded about how their service ended. Somewhere in the chain, blank was converted to text, and the text of a missing value happens to begin with the letter N, which is also a valid exit code. So 26,000 blanks silently became 26,000 confident answers. Nothing crashed. Every total still added up. The true count was about 645.
That is why the checks that run on every build are mostly of the form missing stays missing. A bug that turns absence into a plausible value cannot be caught by looking at the output, because the output looks better than the truth.

8812 """ build_docs.py — generate the single-file HTML documentation site ================================================================ Renders every authored reference document, the tabular crosswalks, and a **live** descriptives + QA sheet into one self-contained ``output/docs/index.html``. Design rule: **nothing is written twice.** ------------------------------------------ The markdown files under ``reference/`` stay the canonical prose; this script only *renders* them. Every number on the Descriptives and QA sheets is **computed from ``data/final`` at build time** — never typed. That is deliberate: the 2026-07-16 audit found that every stale claim in the project (a README two reorgs out of date, a "91 %" that was really 68 %, a documented ``illegitimacy_rate`` that did not exist, a linkage "~90" that was 144) was a hand-maintained copy of a fact that lived somewhere else. A hand-written HTML would have been the most authoritative-looking copy of all. So: if a fact is wrong here, fix its **source** (the markdown, or the pipeline) and rebuild. Do not edit the generated HTML. Contents -------- Overview (README + build stamp + module index) · Descriptives (live) · QA (live invariants) · Pipeline · Place matching · Ranks · Variables · Data dictionary · Census codebook · Data sources · Decisions · Audit. Dependencies: ``markdown``, ``pygments``, ``jinja2`` (all already required). Optional: ``latex2mathml`` → self-contained offline math; without it the page falls back to KaTeX from a CDN (needs a network on first view). Somewhere on a Czech government server there are 133,000 web pages, one per " "legionnaire, each a little table of half-filled fields typed up from a paper card: " "born Kolín, trade zámečník, joined 12.3.1917. A person can read " "one of those in a few seconds. Nobody can read 133,000, and no statistical model can " "read even one — a model wants a rectangle of numbers, and this is a heap of Czech " "sentences.
" "
The pipeline is the machine that turns the heap into the rectangle, and it is " "built in three stages so that each can be checked. Collect: fetch the pages " "and store them exactly as they came, never touched again. Clean: read every " "field with a small specialist — one for dates, one for ranks, one for jobs, one for " "places — and write out a table where a column means the same thing in every row. " "Visualise: draw the pictures, and read only from that final table, so a " "figure can never quietly disagree with the data it claims to show.
" "
The rule that makes the whole thing survivable is that the raw copy is sacred. " "Every judgement — every guess, every repair, every dropped record — happens in the " "middle stage, in code, where it can be read, argued with and undone. If a decision " "made in 2026 turns out to be wrong, the fix is one function and a re-run, not a " "dataset nobody can reconstruct.

Imagine posting a letter addressed only to Nová Ves, Bohemia. There are " "dozens of Nová Ves — New Village is the Czech Springfield — and the one you " "want stopped existing under that name in 1918, was called something else in German, " "and has since been swallowed by a town. That is the problem on every one of these " "birth records, and it has to be solved 300,000 times, because a soldier's birthplace " "is how he gets attached to the 1910 census: how literate his district was, how many " "Czechs and Germans lived in it, how much of it farmed.
" "
So the matcher works like a careful postal clerk rather than a clever one. It " "tries the strongest evidence first — does this string name a district outright? — " "then weaker and weaker readings: a court district, a village in the gazetteer, a " "near-miss spelling. Crucially it writes down which rung it used. Every record " "carries a label saying how confident the match is, so an analysis can throw the weak " "ones away and see whether the result survives.
" "
Two things it refuses to do. It will not break a tie by picking whichever " "candidate the lookup table happened to list first — a coin-flip dressed as an " "answer. And it will not place a village in Slovakia just because a Slovak village " "has the same name, when the record says the man was born in Galicia. Where the " "evidence genuinely runs out, the field stays empty, and empty is a finding.

In 1916 the imperial statistical office printed a book that lists every " "inhabited place in Bohemia — every village, every hamlet, every mill with a name. " "For each one it gives a row of numbers: how many hectares, how many houses, how " "many people, how many Catholics, how many spoke Czech. That part is a spreadsheet " "that happens to be made of paper, and a computer reads it about as well as you " "would expect: nine numbers in ten come out right.
" "
The interesting part is underneath. In tiny type at the foot of every page, the " "book also records what each village had — a school, a midwife, a fire " "brigade, a savings bank, a post office, a Czech credit union rather than a German " "one. That is a completely different kind of fact from a headcount, and nothing else " "in this project comes close to it: you can measure whether a man grew up somewhere " "with institutions or somewhere with none. There is one problem. To save space, the " "1916 typesetter printed those institutions not as words but as little " "pictures — a tiny open book for a school, a stylised helmet for a fire brigade — " "and defined them once, on a key page at the front.
" "
A computer cannot read a picture it has never been shown. Text-recognition " "software sees the school symbol and confidently types g. Modern AI models, " "asked what the mark is, guess — and guess differently from each other: handed the " "identical symbol, two of them answered “doctor” and “curate”. Over one test page " "they agreed with each other about the words of an entry two times in three, " "and about the symbols about one time in ten.
" "
So the work splits in two. The numbers upstairs are read by machine and then " "made to prove themselves: men plus women must equal the total, the villages " "must add up to their parish. Crucially the machine is never told what the answer " "should be — tell it the total and it will happily produce numbers that reach that " "total, and the test stops testing anything. Downstairs there is no such arithmetic, " "nothing adds up to anything, and the only defences are a fixed list of names a " "reader is allowed to use, and a human sitting down with the key page. A person " "reading those marks by hand got 286 of them and was unsure about none, which " "settles one thing at least: the difficulty is not the scan. It is that we are " "asking machines to recognise a picture nobody has drawn for them.

" "
The trap here is a title that is not a grade at all. Some men were entered as " "pracovník (labour service) or občan (civilian) — administrative " "holding categories on the way in, not punishments. Scored naively, a Habsburg " "colonel entering as a labourer looks like the most spectacular demotion in " "the dataset, and it never happened. Those 7,696 records are flagged, and the " "headline result is computed without them.
" ), "ranks-legal" : ( "
When the war ended, hundreds of thousands of men who had worn one uniform had to " "be fitted into another — and the new Czechoslovak state had to decide what their old " "rank was worth. This sheet is the answer, dug out of the statute books.
" "
The law was openly lopsided, and knowing that is the point. Legion service was a " "reward: preferential appointments, generous crediting of time served, " "seniority back-dated as far as 1914. Former Austro-Hungarian officers were let in " "grudgingly and often a grade down. Two men of identical ability ended the decade in " "different places purely because of which army they had been in.
" "
It sits in the documentation because it explains a rumour the data would " "otherwise seem to support. Legionnaires believed officers were being demoted; the " "statutes show the opposite policy. So when the data shows a Habsburg officer entering " "the Legion at a low grade, the explanation is an entry procedure, not a punishment — " "and that distinction changes what the desertion result means.
" ), "units" : ( "
A soldier's record says he served in the 1st Regiment. Which one? The " "Czechoslovak Legion in Russia had a 1st Regiment. So did the Legion in Italy. So did " "the French Foreign Legion, in which a Czech company also fought. Three different " "wars, three different sets of men, one number.
" "
Treating them as one unit would be a real error, not a cosmetic one, because unit " "is how soldiers are grouped for almost every comparison in the project — how big was " "his company, how many of his comrades died, did his regiment desert as a bloc. Mix " "two regiments together and every one of those numbers is wrong.
" "
The fix is to stop using the number alone and use regiment plus army as " "the identity. It sounds trivial; it moved 4,347 records, and it revealed that the " "records labelled 1st Regiment are mostly Foreign Legion rather than the " "Czechoslovak 1st Rifles that everyone assumes.
" ), "habsburg-army" : ( "
The Habsburg army recruited locally on purpose. Each regiment had a home district " "it drew its men from, so a regiment was in effect a slice of one region — its " "language, its trades, its villages. That is the Ergänzung system, and it is " "why a regiment number is quietly also a place.
" "
That link is worth a great deal here. It lets a man's pre-Legion unit be tied " "back to a census district even when his own birthplace field is unreadable, and it " "gives a way to ask whether men from the same home district behaved alike — the kind " "of comparison the whole literature on unit cohesion turns on.
" "
It also explains the ambiguity next door: the Monarchy ran three parallel armies " "— the common army, the Austrian Landwehr and the Hungarian Honvéd — each numbering " "its own regiments from one, each with its own command language. A bare number is " "genuinely ambiguous, which is not sloppiness in the records but a fact about the " "state that kept them.
" ), "provenance" : ( "
A finished number in a paper — desertion in Russia was four percent — hides " "a chain of sources behind it: a scraped website, a census workbook, a shapefile, a " "hand-written dictionary. If any link is weak, the number is weak, and by the time it " "reaches a table nobody can tell which link it was.
" "
This sheet keeps the chain visible. Every mechanism the project claims is drawn " "back to the source that grounds it, so the reader can see at a glance which claims " "rest on an official census, which on a scholarly encyclopedia, and which on a " "judgement made here.
" "
It is also a defence against a specific kind of self-deception: a source used for " "two different purposes starts to look like two independent confirmations. Drawn as a " "graph, that shows up immediately as one node with two arrows out of it — which is " "one piece of evidence, not two.
" ), "architecture" : ( "
This project is about forty Python modules that call each other. That is small " "enough to feel manageable and quite large enough to hide a nasty surprise: you " "change how one function reads a date, and something four steps downstream that you " "had forgotten depends on it starts producing plausible, wrong answers.
" "
So the import graph is drawn automatically from the source itself — never from a " "hand-kept list, which would be out of date within a week. Click a module and the map " "highlights everything that would feel a change to it.
" "
The practical use is before an edit, not after. If the blast radius of a " "one-line change is eleven modules, that is worth knowing while the change is still " "an idea.
" ), "validation-register" : ( "
Most projects report the checks that passed. This one has a column for what each " "check cannot see, and that column is the honest half.
" "
The distinction that organises it: an external check compares this project " "against a source that could genuinely contradict it — a published encyclopedia, an " "official census, an independently trained model. A self-check only confirms " "that the output obeys the rules it was built from. Self-checks are necessary and " "they are not evidence that the coding is right; a rule applied perfectly to the " "wrong data passes every one of them.
" "
Reading the blind-spot column is the fastest way to find out what this project " "does not know. Place matching below the district level, for instance, has no " "external check at all — so it is written down as unchecked rather than left to look " "like it passed.
" ), "validation" : ( "
The best thing that can happen to a dataset is that somebody who has never seen " "it wrote down the answers first. In 2025 a historian published an encyclopedia of " "the Czechoslovak Legions: which units existed, where they fought, when they formed. " "That is an answer key produced with no knowledge of this project whatsoever.
" "
Checked against it, the pipeline's theatre assignment agrees on 99.6  % o f " "records, and every officer rank resolves correctly. More usefully, it found two real " "bugs. The rank ladder had no general grades, so generálmajor matched the word " "major and every Legion general was recorded three rungs too low. And notes " "about a rank — candidate for lieutenant, was not a soldier — " "were being scored as that rank.
" "
It also found roughly 130 records where the source website contradicts the " "historical record: regiments placed in Russia that only ever existed in France. " "Those are documented and left alone. Silently correcting a source is how a dataset " "stops being evidence about the source.
" ), "validation-education" : ( "
What a soldier wrote in the schooling box — ob. 5 mě. 3 and the like — only " "means something if you know what those schools were. Until now that knowledge came " "from two modern history books. Neither counts schools; one of them starts its figures " "in 1924, in a different country.
" "
This page checks the scheme against the thing itself: the Austrian government's own " "annual census of every school it ran, printed in Vienna in 1912 for the year 1908/09, " "with a table for each kind of school in each province and the language it taught in. " "It is the register the ladder should have been built on, and it says three things.
" "
It confirms the awkward call at the heart of the variable. The " "pokračovací school — compulsory evening classes for apprentices — had been " "treated as a rung above the rest, which would have made an apprentice look " "better-educated than a grammar-school boy. The government filed it in a category of " "its own, and it was enormous: 504 of them in Bohemia teaching 50,836 pupils, against " "nine state trade schools teaching 3,518. Leaving it off the ladder was right.
" "
It breaks something else. The code marks an elementary schooling " "“complete” at eight years, because the law required eight years of schooling. " "But the census counts schools by how many year-groups they actually had, and a " "eight-class elementary school existed ten times in the whole empire and twice in " "the Czech lands. Nearly four thousand men are recorded as having finished a school that " "was almost nowhere, and three thousand more who wrote down the ordinary full five years " "are marked as having dropped out. The column is being left alone until that is decided " "properly rather than patched.
" "
And it shows that the evening classes are badly under-recorded: in life there " "were five of those pupils for every full-time trade-school pupil, but in these records " "there are fewer than one. Men simply did not write down the classes they were obliged " "to attend. So that flag counts some apprentices, not all of them.
" "
What none of it touches is Hungary. The volume covers only the Austrian half of the " "monarchy, and about ten thousand men here were schooled in the Hungarian half under " "different laws. That gap is old, and it stays.
" ), "validation-occupations" : ( "
The Czech-to-HISCO dictionary is the part of this project with the most human " "judgement in it, so it gets three independent second opinions, each blind to the " "others — and then two more aimed at the single word that carries a sixth of the " "sample.
" "
The German bridge translates each Czech job into its 1910 German " "equivalent and looks that up in the international database — useful precisely " "because Habsburg records were kept in German, so the translation is contemporary " "rather than modern. OccCANINE is a neural network trained on millions of " "historical job titles in other languages; fed the same German glosses, it agrees on " "88  % o f records at the class level. CZ-ISCO is the modern Czech " "statistical classification — the only source that tests the Czech reading itself " "rather than a translation of it.
" "
Each is blind in a different place, which is the point of having three. The " "German bridge cannot catch a mistranslation. OccCANINE cannot tell a clerk from an " "attendant, because that distinction is administrative and not in the title. CZ-ISCO " "is 2025 usage, so where a trade has drifted in a century it disagrees for the right " "reason and the wrong period — and it reaches none of the old rural words the sample " "is actually full of.
" "
Which leaves the word none of them can reach. Rolník is a sixth of the " "sample and the difference between reading it as a farmer who owns his land and a " "hired farmhand is four social classes. So it gets its own two checks. The 1910 " "census carries columns for whether a man farmed on his own account or for wages, " "district by district: where the census counts more own-account farmers, the " "legionnaires from that district are more owner-coded — which is an argument about " "districts and never about one man. The Vienna Database supplies the missing half, " "because it records people one at a time: among men aged 18–30, a Bauer is " "97.5  % a household head and 0.3  % a son. A farmer's son is not what the " "word names. Wrong territory, and the title and the position were written down by " "the same clerk — so it narrows the doubt rather than closing it.
" ), "decisions" : ( "
Building a dataset means making hundreds of choices that could defensibly have " "gone the other way, and the danger is not making them badly — it is making them " "invisibly. Six months later nobody, including the author, can tell which numbers are " "measurements and which are consequences of a forgotten decision.
" "
So every such choice gets a line here: what was decided, why, and whether it is " "settled, provisional (in force, but the alternative would change " "results) or open. The argument itself is not repeated — it stays in whichever " "document already makes it, and this is the index.
" "
The provisional ones are the interesting ones. They are the places where the " "paper's results depend on a call that a reasonable person could reject, stated in " "advance rather than discovered by a referee.
" ), "audit" : ( "
Twice — once in July 2026 and again in September — the entire codebase was read " "line by line, deliberately looking for reasons to distrust it rather than reasons to " "ship it. This sheet is what the two passes found, newest first.
" "
The September pass found its worst problem in the step that matches a legionnaire " "to the same man in the list of fallen Habsburg soldiers. Two records were called the " "same person when the names were similar enough — but the test scored the whole name " "at once, so a shared first name (there are a great many Františeks) could carry two " "different surnames over the line. A second rule trusted a note field that mostly says " "which regiment keeps the death register, not that the man served in the " "Legion. Once each part of the name had to match on its own and the note had to " "actually mention the Legion, the 2,239 matched men fell to 1,340. Fewer matches, but " "ones that are really the same person.
" "
The July pass found the one below, and it is worth understanding even if you never " "touch the code.
" "
It is the most dangerous shape a data bug takes. About 26,000 soldiers had a blank " "exit field — nothing was recorded about how their service ended. Somewhere in the " "chain, blank was converted to text, and the text of a missing value happens to " "begin with the letter N, which is also a valid exit code. So 26,000 blanks silently " "became 26,000 confident answers. Nothing crashed. Every total still added up. The " "true count was about 645.
" "
That is why the checks that run on every build are mostly of the form missing " "stays missing. A bug that turns absence into a plausible value cannot be caught " "by looking at the output, because the output looks better than the truth.

Stratifying by match tier is the point: the easy tiers ( okres / jaras ) dominate the data, so a plain random sample would barely touch the soft tiers ( fuzzy / settlement / muni ) that carry the real error risk. Here each tier gets a fixed quota, and an unmatched stratum is included to probe false negatives (recall). Why a gate and not just a report Every bug found in the 2026-07-16 audit was silent : the fabricated exit_N produced a perfectly plausible 20 % "Missing" category, and 6,320 double-placed records still carried valid-looking okres names. A check that fails the run is found at the moment it breaks. Hard vs soft A gate that cries wolf gets switched off, so only invariants that should never be violated are hard ( hard=True ): frame exclusivity, key uniqueness, no fabricated codes, no join blow-up, derived columns present. Coordinate accuracy is soft — it can drift for honest external reasons ( Wikidata changes), so it warns rather than fails. Note the scope: these run after the notebook has written data/final , so they cannot prevent bad data being written. What they prevent is unknowingly building on it. Nothing crashed. A check that is only *displayed* is found whenever someone next opens the page — which may be after the figures, tables and regressions have been built on top of it. A check that **fails the run** is found at the moment it breaks. Hard vs soft ------------ A gate that cries wolf gets switched off, so only invariants that should *never* be violated are hard (``hard=True``): frame exclusivity, key uniqueness, no fabricated codes, no join blow-up, derived columns present. Coordinate accuracy is **soft** — it can drift for honest external reasons (Wikidata changes), so it warns rather than fails. Note the scope: these run *after* the notebook has written ``data/final``, so they cannot prevent bad data being written. What they prevent is unknowingly building on it.
